title: The three doors
interaction: Pick one of three doors; the host, who knows where the prize is, opens another to show a goat, and you stay or switch. Play by hand, then let the page play a hundred games with 'always stay' and a hundred with 'always switch', the wins piling into two columns at about two to one. Flip the board to see the three places the prize could be and which choice wins in each, then try ten doors where the host opens eight.
takeaway: Switching wins twice as often as staying, because the first pick is right only one time in three and the host's open door points to the prize the rest of the time.
pitfall: The host must know where the prize is and always open a goat door; if the host opens a door at random and happens to show a goat, the two remaining doors really are equal, and the page should show that case too.
why: The Monty Hall problem is among the most-read probability articles on Wikipedia and a staple of popular maths: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Hall_problem
overlapWith: bayes-theorem: counting a grid of 1,000 people to update on a test result; this page updates on what a host does, with doors and tallies instead of rates and formulas.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A famous puzzle with a real mechanism (what the host knows) that tallies and the three-cases board make clear without formulas; it is distinct from bayes-theorem's base-rate grid.
build 5: A seeded game simulation with stay/switch tallies, an enumeration of prize positions and an n-door generalisation is a tiny, fully honest model.
verifyNote: No catalogue page covers it. bayes-theorem counts test results on a grid of 1,000 people and never models a host's informed choice. The probabilities are correct (2/3 against 1/3), and the pitfall about a random host giving 1/2 is the standard result (Brilliant, Encyclopedia of Math). The model is a simple Monte Carlo with tallies and needs no data. Tallies and counts suit level 0, and the ten-door version is a sound way to build intuition.

title: Shapes that tile a floor
interaction: Pick a shape from the tray (triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) and tap a corner: the page fits copies of the shape around that corner one at a time until it closes the turn, leaves a gap or overlaps. A shape that closes the turn exactly floods the floor with copies; one that does not leaves holes. Then take a square tile and bend one edge: the opposite edge bends to match and the floor still fills, Escher-style.
takeaway: A regular shape (all sides and corners equal) tiles a floor on its own only when copies of its corner fit together into exactly one full turn, which equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons do and regular pentagons and octagons do not.
pitfall: Regular pentagons do not tile, but some irregular pentagons do (fifteen families of convex pentagons are known, and a 2017 proof says there are no more), and every triangle and every four-sided shape tiles. So the page must say 'this regular pentagon', never 'pentagons'.
why: England KS2 maths, Year 5: 'angles at a point and 1 whole turn (total 360°)' is the fact the page rests on; Wikipedia's Tessellation article (regular tilings: only the triangle, square and hexagon, because 3π/5 is not a divisor of 2π) is the demand side. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation
overlapWith: chaos-fractals (level 2) is the nearest page about repeating structure; it repeats across scales, while this page repeats one shape across a flat floor and asks only whether its corners close a full turn.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Fitting corners around a point until they close one full turn is a clear, buildable mechanism that answers a real question and is distinct from chaos-fractals, though it builds on angles-as-turns.

build 5: Fitting regular polygons around a vertex by interior angle, flooding the plane for the three regular tilings, and an Escher tile whose edited edge is translated to the opposite edge are clean geometric constructions.
verifyNote: It is distinct, since no catalogue page covers tiling, and it is level 0 with an L0 prerequisite (angles-as-turns, in the pool). It is buildable as a geometric construction. But the takeaway as written is false for shapes in general. Every triangle and every quadrilateral tiles, and Rao (2017) completed the list of 15 families of convex pentagons that tile. The rule "corners fit into one full turn" only decides the case of regular polygons tiling alone. The takeaway and pitfall need to say "regular". The leadsTo link to states-of-matter is a weak tie but acceptable (crystal lattices).

title: Why triangles are stiff
interaction: Snap sticks together at their ends with pins to make a square, then push on a corner: it leans over into a diamond. Make a triangle and push: nothing moves. Add one diagonal stick to the square and push again; then build a tall tower and a garden gate and find the fewest sticks that stop them wobbling.
takeaway: A triangle is the one shape whose sides fix its corners, so a floppy frame goes stiff the moment a diagonal cuts it into triangles.
pitfall: Stiff is not strong: the page is about shapes holding their angles, not about how much load a stick can carry; do not colour sticks by force or claim triangles 'spread the load'.
why: England KS2 design and technology: 'apply their understanding of how to strengthen, stiffen and reinforce more complex structures' (KS1: 'build structures, exploring how they can be made stronger, stiffer and more stable'). https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-design-and-technology-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-design-and-technology-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: bridges-structures (level 1) loads a bridge and colours members by tension and compression; this page has no loads or forces, only a pin-jointed frame that either keeps its shape or folds.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A square frame folding and a triangle holding firm is a pure mechanism a 10-year-old can build and test, and it is a well-scoped level-0 step before bridges-structures without its forces.

build 4: A pin-jointed stick frame solved by position-based distance constraints (Verlet) shows the square folding and the triangle holding, and a rigidity count can score the fewest-sticks challenge; the solver is level-1 code but the observable is level 0.
verifyNote: It is distinct from bridges-structures, which colours members by tension and compression under load. This page is about the rigidity of a pin-jointed frame (a mechanism against a structure), and the pitfall keeps the two apart. The claim is correct: the pin-jointed triangle is the only polygon that cannot deform, and triangulation makes a frame rigid. A small constraint solver (or springs) that shows the motions still allowed is easy to build in the browser and needs no data. It is honest at level 0 and grounded in the KS1/KS2 design and technology wording on stiffening structures.

title: Cellular automata
interaction: Set the eight bits of a one-dimensional rule by clicking its lookup table, and run it from a single live cell or a random row, each generation drawn as a new line below the last. Rule 90 draws a Sierpinski triangle, rule 30 looks random, rule 110 carries colliding structures, and rule 184 moves cars along a road that jams once more than half the cells are full. Step through all 256 rules and sort them into Wolfram's four classes (die out, repeat, look random, build structures), with a count of live cells over time to compare rules.
takeaway: A rule that only looks at a cell and its two neighbours, applied everywhere at once, can die out, repeat, look random or build moving structures, and changing one bit of the rule can switch between them.
pitfall: Rule 30 looks random but is completely determined: the same starting row always gives the same pattern. And most rules do not make complexity; they die out or repeat, and only a few, like rule 110, build lasting structures.
why: Wikipedia, Elementary cellular automaton and Rule 184 (traffic model): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_184 ; 'Cellular automata' is listed in the catalogue's Reserve.
overlapWith: life-on-a-grid (proposed, level 0): that page plays Conway's two-dimensional Game of Life; this page opens the rule itself as an 8-bit table in one dimension, surveys all 256 rules and their classes, and shows a CA as a traffic model and as a universal computer. chaos-fractals shows complexity in continuous systems; turing-machines uses a tape and head, not a grid of cells updating at once.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A topic promoted from the catalogue's reserve, with editable rules and patterns that emerge from them, honest at level 1 and distinct from chaos-fractals' continuous systems.
build 5: Game of Life on a modest grid and elementary 1D rules from an 8-bit table are exact, cheap algorithms that run at interactive rates in SVG.
verifyNote: Against the existing catalogue it is distinct: chaos-fractals is continuous, and turing-machines is a tape machine. 'Cellular automata' is on the Reserve list, the level is honest for level 1, and the model is trivial to run in the browser. But the selection also contains life-on-a-grid (level 0), which already paints cells, steps Conway's Game of Life, finds blinkers and gliders and edits the rule numbers. Half of this page, and its pitfall about gliders, would repeat that page. The fix narrows this one to what the level-0 page lacks: one-dimensional elementary rules and their 8-bit lookup table, the space of 256 rules and Wolfram's four classes, rule 30's deterministic randomness, rule 90's Sierpinski triangle, rule 184 as a traffic model that conserves cars, and rule 110's universality. Life becomes a level-0 prerequisite (allowed, since it is not above level 1).

title: Exponentials & logarithms
interaction: Fold a strip of paper, breed bacteria or compound interest: a slider sets the growth factor, a counter of doublings runs and the curve shoots off the chart; switch the vertical axis to a log scale and the curve becomes a straight line whose slope is the growth rate. Compare 'add the same amount each step' with 'multiply by the same factor each step' on one chart, read a logarithm as the number of doublings needed, and build a slide rule that multiplies by adding lengths.
takeaway: Growing by a fixed factor each step outruns growing by a fixed amount, and a logarithm just counts how many of those steps it took.
pitfall: Exponential does not mean fast: with a factor just above 1 it starts slowly. And a log-scale line that looks tame is not growth slowing down; say that the rate stays the same.
why: Common Core HSF-LE, Linear, Quadratic and Exponential Models: https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/HSF/LE/
overlapWith: radioactivity: that page shows exponential decay through half-lives and epidemics shows cases doubling; this page isolates the rule itself, puts growth and decay on one log axis, and defines the logarithm as a count of steps.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: build 5: Repeated multiplication, a linear/log axis toggle and a slide rule made of log-length bars are closed-form geometry with no data, a small, honest level-1 model.

fit-level 4: A core gap: radioactivity and epidemics use exponentials but no page isolates multiply-versus-add growth or explains the log as a count of steps. The slide rule and log axis give the graphic a real mechanism to show.
verifyNote: The catalogue's Reserve names this topic. radioactivity (half-life decay), epidemics (case doubling) and rockets (the rocket equation) each use an exponential inside a mechanism, but none isolates growth by a constant factor, the log axis or the logarithm as a count of steps. The overlapping pool entry growing-patterns (level 0) was not selected. Level 1 is honest: Common Core HSF-LE puts exponential models and logarithms as solutions of a*b^(ct)=d in high school. It runs as pure arithmetic, curves and a slide-rule construction. The takeaway is sound, reading a logarithm as the count of factor steps, fractional counts included. The pitfall is a real misconception, correctly stated. Small improvement: the entry says the log-scale slope 'is the growth rate'; strictly it is the logarithm of the growth factor per step, so the narrative should phrase it as 'a fixed growth factor'.

title: Game theory: why cooperate?
interaction: Play the prisoner's dilemma against the page with a payoff table whose four numbers can be edited, and find that cheating pays once but not when the same two players meet again. Enter strategies (always cheat, always cooperate, tit for tat, grudger, random) into a round-robin tournament of repeated games and watch the scores; let the population evolve, with well-scoring strategies copied more often, and add a little noise to the signals to see which strategies survive it. Finish on a grid where each cell plays its neighbours, so that clusters of cooperators grow or are eaten.
takeaway: When the same players meet again and again, strategies that start nice, hit back and forgive can outscore pure selfishness, so cooperation can take hold among players who each look after only themselves, unless the games are too short or too few others cooperate.
needsSource: none
pitfall: Tit for tat never beat an opponent in a single game; it won the tournaments by scoring well with everyone. There is no best strategy independent of the population it plays in, and the result changes with the payoff numbers and with noise.
why: Nicky Case's 'The Evolution of Trust', an interactive built on Axelrod's tournaments https://ncase.me/trust/ (coverage: https://boingboing.net/2017/07/26/fun-interactive-game-theory-si.html )
overlapWith: evolution runs selection on a heritable trait and ecosystems couples populations; here the agents choose, with payoffs. The pool's evolutionary-game-theory (level 3) is the replicator ODE on the simplex; this is the level-1 tournament-and-grid version with no equation.
judgeNotes: build 5: An Axelrod-style round-robin of five fixed strategies, a copy-the-winner population update and a spatial grid game are cheap agent simulations that run easily in the browser, and the honest model needs no equations at level 1.

fit-level 4: An Axelrod tournament is a vivid, popular mechanism with no existing equivalent and is honest at level 1. Its spatial-grid finale duplicates the one in evolutionary-game-theory, so the grid belongs on only one of the two pages.
verifyNote: Distinct from the catalogue: evolution has no choosing agents or payoffs, and reinforcement-learning is a single agent. 'Game theory' is on the Reserve list, and the level-3 replicator-dynamics entries (evolutionary-games, evolutionary-game-theory) were not selected. Level 1 is honest. The model is an exact algorithm: an iterated prisoner's dilemma round-robin, imitation dynamics, and a Nowak-May spatial grid. The pitfall is factually right: Axelrod himself notes tit for tat never did better than the player it faced and won on total score. The 2014 reanalysis (PMC4520619) confirms its success depends on payoffs, tournament design and noise. The takeaway, though, states a universal law ('beats pure selfishness') that the entry's own pitfall contradicts: under noise, or among enough defectors, tit for tat loses. The fix softens the takeaway to 'can outscore', with the conditions observable in the toy.

title: Differential equations
interaction: Choose a rule for the slope at every point (growth in proportion to the amount, cooling toward room temperature, logistic growth with a ceiling, a fish stock under steady harvesting) and the plane of time against amount fills with small slope arrows; click anywhere to drop a starting value and watch a solution curve thread through the arrows. Drop several starts and see that curves never cross, that some settle on a level line and others run away from it, and raise the harvest until the level line vanishes and every curve crashes; where an exact formula exists, overlay it on the traced curve.
takeaway: A differential equation says how fast something changes given where it is, and that rule plus a starting point fixes one curve through the field of arrows, which can be followed even when no formula exists.
needsSource: none
pitfall: Not every differential equation can be solved with a formula: most cannot, and the slope field still fixes each solution. Solution curves of one equation never cross, so two different futures cannot start from the same state.
why: 3Blue1Brown, 'Differential equations, a tourist's guide' (over 4 million views) https://www.classcentral.com/classroom/youtube-differential-equations-a-tourist-s-guide-133384 ; AP Calculus BC Unit 7 (slope fields, Euler's method) https://fiveable.me/ap-calc/unit-7.md
overlapWith: calculus finds the slope and area of a given curve; this page starts from the slope rule and finds the curve. phase-portraits (proposed, level 3) owns two-variable systems such as springs and predator–prey; this page is the one-variable slope field, equilibria and their stability.
judgeNotes: build 5: Slope fields and Euler or exact solution curves for the four named equations are a few arithmetic operations per arrow, a small honest model with no data.

fit-level 4: Slope fields with Euler stepping are the natural sequel to calculus and a true level-2 page, one of the few justified at that level. Keep the step-size blow-up brief so it doesn't duplicate numerical-stability.
verifyNote: This is a Reserve topic, and level 2 is honest (AP Calculus BC Unit 7 covers slope fields and Euler's method). Three problems remain. (a) Stepping by hand with Euler's method, shrinking the step and watching it converge or blow up is the whole of the proposed how-simulations-work (L1), and numerical-stability (L3) covers the blow-up, so the page would repeat both. (b) The spring and rabbits-and-foxes are second-order or two-variable systems: they cannot be drawn as a slope field in the (t, y) plane, and as phase-plane flows they belong to phase-portraits. (c) The pitfall overstates its case: a formula, when one exists, is a solution; the point is that most equations have none. Fix: keep the page to first-order equations dy/dt = f(t, y) and to slope fields and solution curves, with Euler only as 'follow the arrows'.
linkLog: dropped related phase-portraits (it lists this topic as a prerequisite)

title: The brachistochrone & calculus of variations
interaction: Drag the control points of a ramp between two fixed points and a bead slides down it under gravity, its descent time computed by integrating along the curve; race the straight line, a circular arc and your curve. Press optimize and the curve relaxes step by step toward the cycloid as the page descends the gradient of the time functional, while a panel shows the Euler–Lagrange residual along the curve going to zero; a second example finds the hanging-chain shape.
takeaway: The fastest slide between two points is a curve, the cycloid, not the straight line, and at the optimum the Euler–Lagrange residual is zero all along the curve, so no small change to its shape makes the slide faster.
pitfall: The best curve can dip below the end point and still win (it does whenever the horizontal distance is more than about π/2 times the drop), and the straight line is not 'almost as good': show it losing to the cycloid by a measured margin. A curve that satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation is stationary, not automatically the minimum.
why: Fowler, Graduate Classical Mechanics, ch. 2 'The Calculus of Variations' (brachistochrone): https://phys.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Classical_Mechanics/Graduate_Classical_Mechanics_(Fowler)/02%3A_The_Calculus_of_Variations/2.05%3A_Fastest_Curve_for_Given_Horizontal_Distance ; demand: myPhysicsLab brachistochrone simulation https://www.myphysicslab.com/roller/brachistochrone-en.html
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page sends a cart along an editable track with energy bars; this page asks which track is best and finds it by varying the whole curve.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: build 5: The bead's descent time is a 1D quadrature along a spline, and gradient descent on a dozen control points converging to the analytic cycloid (plus the catenary) runs at interactive rates; this is the real functional being minimised.

fit-level 4: The brachistochrone race is a classic, visual, wanted subject, and relaxing a curve toward the cycloid shows the real functional being minimized. That is honest level-3 content and distinct from newtons-laws.
verifyNote: Distinct: newtons-laws runs a cart along an editable track, but nothing in the catalogue optimises over whole curves. Level 3 is honest, because the brachistochrone and the catenary are standard material in university classical mechanics and calculus-of-variations courses. The model is real and cheap: the descent time is integrated along a discretised curve (the 1/sqrt(y) singularity at the start can be integrated), and gradient descent on a few dozen nodes runs at interactive rates. The catenary needs a length constraint (a Lagrange multiplier), which is also tractable. The pitfall is correct: the path dips below the end point when the horizontal distance exceeds π/2 times the drop. Two small fixes. The Euler–Lagrange equation is necessary, not sufficient, so the takeaway should say the optimum makes it hold rather than that a curve holding it beats every neighbour. And a brachistochrone is not an everyday object.

title: Phase portraits & stability
interaction: Drag the four entries of a 2×2 linear system, or move its two eigenvalues on the complex plane, and the phase plane redraws as a node, saddle, spiral or center while a trace–determinant chart marks where you are. Switch to a nonlinear system (damped pendulum, predator–prey, van der Pol) and hover a critical point to see its linearization laid over the real flow; drag a parameter through a Hopf bifurcation and watch a limit cycle be born.
takeaway: Near a fixed point whose eigenvalues have nonzero real parts, the real flow looks like its linearization, so a few fixed points and their eigenvalues sketch the whole portrait; when the eigenvalues reach the imaginary axis, as at a Hopf bifurcation, the nonlinear terms take over and a limit cycle can appear that no fixed point predicts.
pitfall: A center predicted by the linearization is not conclusive: the nonlinear terms decide (Hartman–Grobman covers only hyperbolic points). Show the frictionless pendulum beside the damped one rather than claiming linearization settles every case.
why: MIT OCW 18.03SC, Unit IV, Linearization near critical points (including its structural-stability note on borderline centers): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/pages/unit-iv-first-order-systems/linearization-near-critical-points
overlapWith: chaos-fractals shows sensitivity to initial conditions and the logistic map's cascade, and the pool's hamiltonian-phase-space is about area preservation and Poincaré sections; this page classifies flows in the plane by their fixed points and eigenvalues and shows where linearization stops working (ecosystems shows one predator–prey cycle at level 1 as curves, not as a portrait).
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: build 5: Eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix, a trace–determinant chart, a streamline field and RK4 trajectories for the pendulum, predator–prey and van der Pol systems through a Hopf bifurcation all run live, with no data.

fit-level 4: Classifying flows by eigenvalues on the trace-determinant chart, with linearizations laid over real flows and a Hopf bifurcation, is the standard university model. It is distinct from chaos-fractals and ecosystems.
verifyNote: Distinct enough and honestly at level 3: it is MIT 18.03 Unit IV. hamiltonian-phase-space (pool, L3) is about preserved area and Poincaré sections, not about classifying fixed points. The model is cheap to run in the browser. But the takeaway is factually wrong and contradicts the entry's own pitfall. 'Near each fixed point the real flow is the linear flow' holds only at hyperbolic points (Hartman–Grobman); at centers, and at the Hopf bifurcation the page itself shows, it fails (MIT 18.03SC's structural-stability note gives a linearised center that settles nothing). 'Long-run behavior read off from a few fixed points' also ignores the limit cycles the page creates. Fix the takeaway, and add the proposed L2 differential-equations as a prerequisite.

title: Random graphs & the giant component
interaction: Slide the average degree of a random graph and watch components merge, coloured by size: the largest component's share of the nodes stays near zero until the average degree passes 1, then climbs, plotted live against degree. Raise the number of nodes from 50 to a few thousand and rerun the sweep: the curve's knee at degree 1 sharpens toward a corner. A second view opens bonds on a square grid at random and shows a spanning cluster appearing at its own threshold, near half the bonds open.
takeaway: In a large random network, adding links does not connect it gradually: a giant connected piece appears abruptly once each node has about one link on average, and the bigger the network, the sharper that switch.
pitfall: The sharp threshold is a large-graph limit; with a few hundred nodes the curve is rounded. Show the knee sharpening as n grows instead of drawing a step.
why: MIT 6.207/14.15 Networks, Lecture 4: Erdős–Rényi graphs and phase transitions: https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/inline-files/Lecture%204%20-%20Erdos-Renyi%20Graphs%20and%20Phase%20Transitions.pdf
overlapWith: internet: that page routes packets across a given network and epidemics spreads infection through a crowd; this page is about the structure of random networks and the threshold at which they connect at all.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: build 5: Erdős–Rényi graphs on a few hundred nodes with union-find for the giant component, preferential attachment and grid bond percolation are cheap seeded simulations, and the threshold appears in the live plot.

fit-level 4: The giant component's sudden appearance at average degree 1 is a striking emergent mechanism, and preferential attachment adds real network science. No existing page covers network structure itself.
verifyNote: Distinct from every existing page (internet routes packets over a fixed network, epidemics has an R0 threshold in time not a structural one, pagerank ranks a hand-built web); Erdos-Renyi with a few hundred nodes and union-find runs at interactive rates; level 3 is honest (network science / random graph theory course, MIT 6.207). Two weaknesses: the page tries three toys (ER, preferential attachment, grid percolation), and preferential attachment's takeaway (hubs) is a different idea not observable in the same graphic; and the takeaway says 'suddenly' while the pitfall rightly says a finite graph is rounded. Narrow to ER with a node-count control so the knee sharpening is the thing seen, keep grid percolation as the second view of the same threshold, and qualify the takeaway.

title: The bootstrap & permutation tests
interaction: Compare flipper length between two species of real penguins: shuffle the group labels thousands of times to build the histogram of differences that chance alone produces, and read the p-value as where the observed difference falls in it. Resample each group with replacement to build a bootstrap distribution and a confidence interval for the difference and for a regression slope. Then switch to a known simulated population, repeat the whole procedure hundreds of times, and count how often the interval catches the true value: drag the sample size down, skew the population or ask for the maximum instead of the mean, and watch the coverage fall below 95%.
takeaway: Resampling rebuilds the chance distribution from the data itself, and it works only as well as the sample stands in for the population: with small or skewed samples the intervals miss the truth more often than they claim.
needs: The Palmer penguins dataset (344 penguins, bill and flipper measurements by species; palmerpenguins, CC0).
pitfall: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a bootstrap interval is not guaranteed to have its stated coverage: the bootstrap does not cure a small sample. The coverage counter must show the shortfall, not a reassuring 95%.
why: Hesterberg, What Teachers Should Know about the Bootstrap: Resampling in the Undergraduate Statistics Curriculum: https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.5279
overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits a curve and shows overfitting with a held-out set; this page asks whether a difference or slope is real by rebuilding the chance distribution from the data, and how often the resulting intervals actually catch the truth.
needsSource: Palmer penguins (Gorman, Williams & Fraser 2014; palmerpenguins package): CC0
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Permutation tests, the bootstrap and power are real university statistics with a mechanism the graphic shows directly (rebuilding the null distribution), and the page is clearly distinct from central-limit-theorem and learning-from-data.

build 5: Permutation tests, bootstrap and power curves are a few thousand cheap resamples of 344 rows, an honest algorithm at interactive rates; palmerpenguins is confirmed CC0 (the authors ask, as a courtesy and not a licence term, to be contacted before publication).
verifyNote: Data is fine (palmerpenguins is CC0, confirmed). But two problems. Duplication: the power plot, the false-positive rate and the 'run twenty null comparisons and one is significant' demo are exactly the core of the proposed level-3 clinical-trials page (power, false positives, multiple outcomes, early stopping). Level: p-values, power and Type I error, and even simulation-based permutation tests, are AP Statistics / first-year intro-stats material (Hesterberg's cited paper is about the undergraduate intro curriculum), i.e. level 2, not level 3. A small change fixes both: narrow to resampling itself and make it genuinely university-level by checking the bootstrap against a known population, where its interval coverage can be measured and seen to fall short at small n or for statistics like the maximum (Efron & Tibshirani; Hesterberg 2015 notes percentile intervals undercover for small n).

title: Taylor series & where they stop working
interaction: Pick a function and add Taylor terms one at a time with a slider: the polynomial hugs e^x and sin x ever further from the center, but for 1/(1 + x²) it closes in only for |x| < 1 and swings ever wilder beyond, however many terms are added. A linked complex plane shows the disk of convergence and the function's singularities at ±i: the disk stops exactly where it touches the nearest one; drag the center along the real line and the disk, and the stretch of the real line the polynomials fit, resize to match. A last toggle overlays Chebyshev interpolation, which fits the whole interval anyway.
takeaway: The Taylor series of a function converges exactly out to its nearest singularity in the complex plane, even when nothing goes wrong on the real line.
pitfall: More terms do not always mean a better fit: outside the radius each new term makes the polynomial worse, and a function can be smooth everywhere on the real line and still have a finite radius. Do not claim convergence on the boundary circle: for 1/(1 + x²) the series diverges at x = ±1.
why: 3Blue1Brown, Essence of calculus: Taylor series: https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/taylor-series
overlapWith: calculus: that page shows the tangent line (the first Taylor term) and the integral; this page stacks the higher terms and explains the radius of convergence through the complex plane.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Showing the radius of convergence set by a complex singularity is a real and surprising mechanism; plain Taylor polynomials would be level 2, but the complex-disk explanation makes level 3 honest, and it is distinct from calculus.
build 5: Partial sums, the disk of convergence reaching the singularities at ±i, and Chebyshev interpolation are exact cheap computations, and blow-up beyond |x| = 1 is visible at a glance.
verifyNote: Not a duplicate: calculus shows only tangent and area; fourier-transform sums sines, not powers. Level is borderline: Taylor polynomials and radius/interval of convergence are AP Calculus BC (high school) material, which alone would be level 2; what makes it level 3 is explaining the radius by the nearest complex singularity (complex analysis), so that disk must be the core, not a side panel. One factual slip: the series for 1/(1+x^2) does not 'fit perfectly up to |x| = 1'; it converges only for |x| < 1, slowly near 1, and diverges at |x| = 1 itself. Takeaway should say the function is analytic at the centre. All buildable as closed-form polynomials; prerequisites calculus and complex-numbers are level 2, fine.

title: Why the sky is blue & sunsets red
interaction: Scrub the Sun across a day's sky: a patch of sky overhead and the Sun's own disc take the colours that come out when sunlight scatters off air along its path, worked out colour by colour from the real sunlight spectrum and shown as screen colours. Thicken the air or add smoke and the sunset deepens to orange and the daytime sky goes paler. Pump the air away altogether and the sky turns black around a white Sun, as on the Moon.
takeaway: Air scatters blue light out of sunlight far more than red, so the sky overhead is blue and the Sun turns red when its light has crossed a lot of air near the horizon.
needs: None that needs a licence: sunlight above the air as a Planck spectrum at the Sun's effective temperature (5772 K, the IAU nominal value), and the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions from the analytic fit of Wyman, Sloan & Shirley (JCGT 2013), a formula. Optional, once its licence is confirmed: the ASTM G173-03 AM0 'Etr' column from NLR/NREL as a cited cross-check.
