title: Floating, sinking & boats
interaction: Lower objects into a brim-full tank (a stone, an apple, a wooden block, a steel ball, a ball of modelling clay): the water each one pushes aside spills into a cup on a scale, and a spring balance holding the object shows it getting lighter as it goes in. Each one sinks, or settles where the spilled water weighs as much as it does. Reshape the clay from a ball into a bowl and the same lump floats; load it with marbles until it goes under. Change the water to salt water or to oil and see who floats now; finally warm the air inside a balloon and watch it rise through the surrounding air the same way.
takeaway: A thing floats if it can push aside its own weight of water (or air) before it is completely under, which is why the same lump of clay sinks as a ball and floats as a bowl.
needs: A handful of handbook densities (water, sea water, oil, ice, wood, steel, air).
pitfall: Heavy things do not simply sink and light things float: a steel ship floats and a grain of sand sinks; what matters is the weight compared with the weight of the water pushed aside.
why: Bartosz Ciechanowski, 'Naval Architecture' (interactive explainer on why ships float) https://ciechanow.ski/naval-architecture/ ; KS3 physics 'Pressure in fluids' (upthrust effects, floating and sinking) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ; PhET 'Density' listed in the PhET middle-school guide https://phet.colorado.edu/files/guides/MiddleSchool_en.pdf and 'Buoyancy: Basics' on PhET's fluids search page https://phet.colorado.edu/en/search?q=fluids
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page shows ice being less dense than water inside a molecular box; this one is about whole objects in a tank, the water they push aside and why a bowl of clay floats when a ball of it sinks.
needsSource: Archimedes' principle with the submerged area of a draggable hull computed from the water line; densities from a handbook table (Wikipedia's density tables, CC BY-SA 4.0, or a physics textbook; the few values are not copyrightable facts).
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Floating explained by the weight of the water pushed aside, with the clay ball and clay bowl, is a must-have formula-free mechanism that no existing page covers.
build 5: Solving for the waterline where the displaced area's weight equals the object's weight on a 2D hull polygon is an honest, fast model, and a few handbook densities are uncopyrightable facts.
verifyNote: Distinct from the catalogue: states-of-matter only shows ice less dense than water inside a molecular box, and flight is about lift, not buoyancy. Level 0 is honest (KS3 upthrust, PhET Buoyancy Basics), and the model (Archimedes with a waterline from a hull's cross-section) is easily buildable. Handbook densities are facts. Note for the curator: the pool also has sink-or-float (chemistry) and fluid-pressure-buoyancy (physics), so these are probably to be merged or chosen between. Two factual faults. (1) The takeaway says a thing floats when it pushes aside MORE than its own weight. A floating object pushes aside exactly its own weight. The rule is that it floats if it can push aside its own weight before it is completely under, and as written the takeaway invites the opposite misconception. (2) A 'scale under the tank' does not show the pushed-aside water: for a stone resting on the bottom, it rises by the stone's whole weight. The honest instrument is an overflow (eureka) can spilling into a cup on a scale, set beside a spring balance holding the object.

title: Magnets & poles
interaction: Drag two bar magnets about on a board: arrows show the pull or push between them, computed from their poles, and a compass needle and a sprinkle of iron filings line up along the field. Flip one magnet end for end and the pull turns into a push. Slide a steel paper clip toward a magnet to see it become a magnet of its own and pick up a chain of clips, then cut a magnet in half and find that each half still has two ends.
takeaway: A magnet always has two ends; like ends push apart and unlike ends pull together, and the pull fades quickly with distance.
pitfall: A magnet does not attract all metals, nor even all steel: it pulls iron, nickel, cobalt and most steels, but not aluminium, copper, gold or many stainless-steel spoons and sinks. And cutting a magnet never separates its poles: each piece has two.
why: NGSS 3-PS2-3 (electric or magnetic interactions between objects not in contact; the clarification names paper clips and magnets) https://www2.cde.ca.gov/cacs/id/web/29018 ; KS2 Year 3 'Forces and magnets' (magnets have two poles; predict whether two magnets attract or repel) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: electromagnetism: that page (level 2) places charges, draws field lines and induces currents with coils; this one has no electricity at all, only permanent magnets, their two poles, what they attract and how a clip becomes a temporary magnet.
needsSource: none; the model is the two-pole (Gilbert) bar magnet with inverse-square pole forces and an induced pole pair for steel.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core primary-school subject with a real mechanism (poles, falling-off pull, induced magnetism in a clip); it is fully level 0 and distinct from the level-2 electromagnetism page, and it is a natural lead-in to it.

build 4: A Gilbert two-pole model with inverse-square forces, a field sampled for the compass and filings, and an induced pole pair for steel clips are all cheap to compute, and an honest level-0 approximation as long as the page notes that poles are a model.
verifyNote: Distinct from electromagnetism (level 2: charges, field lines, induction), and squarely NGSS 3-PS2-3 / KS2 Year 3. Level 0 is honest. The Gilbert two-pole model with inverse-square pole forces, a field-direction field for the filings and compass, and an induced dipole in steel is a real, cheap model; it needs no data. Note for the curator: the pool also has magnets-and-electromagnets (physics) and compass-and-magnetic-poles (earth), which overlap at this level. The fault is the pitfall: 'only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt' repeats a misconception. Common austenitic stainless steels (304/316, cutlery and sinks) are not attracted or only barely, while many alloys and some rare-earth metals are. The takeaway and the cut-magnet point are correct.

title: Shadows & pinholes
interaction: Drag a lamp, a toy and a wall about a room: straight rays from the lamp are blocked by the toy, and the shadow on the wall grows as the lamp comes closer and shrinks as the wall comes closer. Swap the small bulb for a wide lampshade and the shadow's edge goes soft; switch on a second lamp and a second shadow appears. Poke a pinhole in a shoebox and the picture of the lamp forms upside down on its back wall.
takeaway: Light travels in straight lines, so a shadow is simply where the lines are blocked, and its size follows the lines back to the lamp.
pitfall: A shadow is not something a lamp throws onto a wall; it is where no light arrives. And the Moon's phases are not Earth's shadow (the page should point to sun-earth-moon for eclipses, which are).
why: Bartosz Ciechanowski, 'Lights and Shadows' https://ciechanow.ski/lights-and-shadows/ ; KS2 Year 3 'Light' (find patterns in the way the size of shadows change) and Year 6 'Light' (light appears to travel in straight lines; shadows have the shape of the objects that cast them) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: light-optics: that page bends rays through lenses and prisms on an optical bench; this one never bends a ray, only blocks it, and is about shadow size, soft edges and the pinhole picture.
needsSource: none; ray projection from a point or extended source past polygons onto a wall (umbra and penumbra).
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Straight-line light explaining shadow size, soft edges and the pinhole image is core KS2 content, shown purely by geometry, and it never overlaps the refraction bench.
build 5: 2D ray projection from point and extended sources past polygons gives the umbra, penumbra and pinhole inversion exactly, and it is cheap and fully honest.
verifyNote: Distinct from light-optics, which only bends rays through lenses and prisms; blocking rays, umbra and penumbra, and the pinhole image are not on any page, and the eclipse case stays with sun-earth-moon. The level is honest: KS2 Year 3 and Year 6 'Light' cover this, it needs no formulas, and shadow size is a comparison. Ray projection past polygons from a point source or an extended one is a cheap geometric model and needs no data. The takeaway and the pitfall (shadow as an absence of light; phases are not Earth's shadow) are both correct.

title: Vibrations & sound
interaction: Twang a ruler held over the edge of a table: the strip wobbles, and a row of air particles passes the push along to an ear, each one jiggling in place while the squeeze travels down the row; the speakers play the note. Slide the ruler in to shorten it and the wobble quickens and the note rises; twang it harder and the wobble widens and the note gets louder. Move the ear away and the sound fades, then pump the air out of a jar around a ringing bell and nothing arrives at all.
takeaway: A sound is a wobble passed along through the air: a faster wobble is a higher note, a bigger wobble a louder one, and with nothing in between to pass it on, nothing reaches the ear.
pitfall: Sound does not travel as air flying from the source to the ear; each bit of air jiggles in place and passes the push on. Louder is not higher: loudness and pitch are two different things. Sound needs some material to carry it, not air in particular: it travels through water, wood and metal too, and only empty space stops it.
why: KS2 Year 4 'Sound' (sounds are made by something vibrating; vibrations travel through a medium to the ear; sounds get fainter with distance) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ; Bartosz Ciechanowski, 'Sound' https://ciechanow.ski/sound/
overlapWith: waves-interference: that page puts two sources in a ripple tank and finds a string's harmonics; this one has a single vibrating ruler and a single row of air particles, no interference, no harmonics, just pitch, loudness, distance and the need for air.
needsSource: none; a vibrating strip whose rate rises as it is shortened (cantilever), a one-dimensional chain of masses and springs for the air, loudness falling with distance, and synthesised tones through Web Audio.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core KS2/KS3 and NGSS subject with a clear mechanism (vibration passed along through air: pitch, loudness, the bell jar) that is a true beginner on-ramp to waves-interference and does not duplicate its interference and harmonics.

build 4: Cantilever frequency scaling as 1/L squared, a 1D mass-spring chain for the air, distance falloff and Web Audio tones are all small and honest. The bell jar works by reducing the chain's coupling and density.
verifyNote: Distinct from waves-interference, which has two sources, harmonics and Doppler but never shows what sound is: one vibrating source, a longitudinal push passed along a chain, the need for a medium. The level fits KS2 Year 4, and a ruler that sounds higher when shortened (f ~ 1/L^2) plus a mass-spring chain is a real model. One small flaw: the takeaway says 'with no air nothing reaches the ear', which teaches that sound needs air specifically. Sound also travels through solids and water (the bell jar's stand leaks some), so the claim should be that it needs some material to pass the push along. Fixed by rewording the takeaway and adding this to the pitfall.

title: Why music has twelve notes
interaction: A keyboard whose keys play, each note drawn as its wave; press two keys and the page plays them together and draws how the waves line up: an octave (double the frequency) repeats every cycle, a fifth (3:2) every two, while clashing pairs beat and a roughness meter (the Plomp-Levelt curve) rises. Slide a divider to cut the octave into 5, 7, 12, 19, 31 or 53 equal steps and read off how many cents each ladder misses the pure fifth and major third by; twelve is the first small ladder whose fifth lands within 2 cents. Compare an equal-tempered chord with a pure one by ear.
takeaway: Notes sound smooth together when their frequencies are in simple ratios, and twelve equal steps per octave is the smallest small ladder whose fifth lands almost exactly on the pure 3:2.
pitfall: Twelve is a good compromise, not a law of nature or of the ear: other traditions divide the octave differently, and equal temperament makes every fifth slightly flat. Consonance also depends on timbre; the roughness model (Plomp-Levelt 1965) is one measurable part of it.
why: 'Why 12 notes to the octave?' (University of Waterloo) is a widely read answer to a perennial question: https://www.math.uwaterloo.ca/~mrubinst/tuning/12.html
overlapWith: waves-interference: beats and a string's harmonics; this page is which pairs of notes fit together and why the octave is cut into twelve.
needsSource: none (tones synthesized in the browser; the Plomp-Levelt roughness curve is a published formula)
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: An appealing, distinctive question with a real mechanism (frequency ratios, beats and a roughness model, dividing the octave equally) that waves-interference does not cover, at an honest level 1.

build 5: Equal-division arithmetic, the Plomp-Levelt/Sethares roughness formula, waveform overlays and Web Audio synthesis form a real, tiny model whose results (the 12-EDO fifth within 2 cents) are visible and audible.
verifyNote: Distinct from waves-interference, which covers beats and string harmonics but not which intervals fit together or how the octave is divided. Level 1 is fair (frequency ratios and logarithmic steps), synthesized tones plus the published Plomp-Levelt roughness curve make an honest model, and no data is needed. The takeaway overclaims in two ways. First, 5- and 7-step divisions also land within about 20 cents of the fifth, so twelve is not simply 'the smallest ladder that lands close'. What makes 12 special is that 7/12 is a continued-fraction convergent of log2(3/2), putting its fifth within 2 cents (the next good ones are 41 and 53). Second, the twelve-key keyboard came from chains of fifths in Pythagorean and meantone tunings, centuries before equal temperament, so equal temperament is not why pianos have twelve keys. Fixed by narrowing the takeaway and the interaction to what the graphic shows.

title: The Ising model & phase transitions
interaction: Run a square lattice of spins with the Metropolis algorithm (or the Wolff cluster update, which stays fast near the critical point) and slide the temperature through Tc: domains grow out of noise, the magnetization rises steeply but continuously from zero as the lattice cools below Tc, and the susceptibility and heat capacity spike. Below Tc, apply a field and sweep it back and forth to trace a hysteresis loop; grow the lattice to see the peaks sharpen, and shrink it to a one-dimensional chain to see the transition vanish.
takeaway: In two dimensions, nearest-neighbour alignment alone produces a phase transition at a definite temperature, sharp only in the limit of a large system, while a one-dimensional chain never orders.
pitfall: A one-dimensional chain has no phase transition at any temperature above zero; show that case so the reader does not believe order is automatic.
why: MIT OCW RES.8-010 Introduction to Statistical Physics, lecture 8 on the Ising model via its partition function: https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-8-010-introduction-to-statistical-physics-summer-2018/mitres_8_010su18_lec8.pdf
overlapWith: states-of-matter: freezes and boils a box of molecules; this page strips a transition down to the simplest possible model and shows the critical point's divergences.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The canonical stat-mech model of a phase transition, with a clear Metropolis mechanism and the 1D no-transition case; it is distinct from states-of-matter.

build 5: A Metropolis 2D lattice of a few hundred spins on a side runs easily at interactive rates, and every claimed observation (domains, susceptibility peak, hysteresis, no 1D transition) comes straight out of it.
verifyNote: Distinct from states-of-matter, a level-1 molecular-dynamics box with no critical point or divergences. Level 3 is honest (statistical physics courses cover it, e.g. MIT OCW RES.8-010), its prerequisites are entropy (level 2) and the proposed level-3 partition-function, and Metropolis on a 2D lattice runs easily in the browser. Two physics errors. (a) The interaction says the magnetization 'jumps from zero to nearly full' at Tc, but the 2D Ising transition is continuous (second order): it rises steeply and continuously (beta = 1/8) as T falls below Tc. A jump would teach the first-order picture. (b) The takeaway says nearest-neighbour alignment 'alone' gives a sharp transition, yet the page itself shows that the one-dimensional chain has none, so dimension (at least two) must be in the takeaway. Also: near Tc, single-flip Metropolis slows down sharply (critical slowing down), so offer a Wolff cluster update, and the hysteresis loop only appears below Tc.

title: Lasers
interaction: Pump a four-level gain medium between two mirrors and watch the populations and the photon number evolve under the rate equations: below threshold the cavity holds a few spontaneous photons, and at threshold the inversion clamps while the output climbs linearly with pump power. Lower the mirror reflectivity, switch to a three-level or a two-level medium, or open and close a shutter to see relaxation oscillations and a Q-switched pulse.
takeaway: A laser is a cavity in which stimulated emission out-competes loss, and above that threshold the inversion stops growing and nearly every extra pumped atom adds a photon to the same mode.
pitfall: Population inversion is impossible by pumping a two-level system at any power; the page must show the two-level case saturating at equal populations.
why: PhET 'Lasers' is in its quantum collection, and MIT OCW 6.977 builds threshold and inversion from the rate equations: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-977-semiconductor-optoelectronics-theory-and-design-fall-2002/
overlapWith: solar-cells: a junction turns photons into current; this is the inverse, a medium amplifying light, and the LED half of the Reserve item is a sentence in semiconductors, not a page.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: High visitor demand and a real rate-equation model (threshold, clamping, two-level saturation, Q-switching) that no existing page covers.
build 5: Four-level rate equations with a photon number are a small, stiff-but-easy ODE that shows threshold, clamping, relaxation oscillations and Q-switching honestly.
verifyNote: Not in the catalogue; it is the 'Lasers & LEDs' item in the Reserve list, and nearest pages (solar-cells, semiconductors) do not show stimulated emission, cavity threshold or inversion. Level 3 is honest (rate equations, Q-switching and relaxation oscillations are university laser-physics material, e.g. MIT 6.977), and its prerequisites (quantum-mechanics, level 3; oscillations-resonance, level 1) are within level. A few coupled rate-equation ODEs integrate easily at interactive rates, and no data is needed. The pitfall is correct (steady incoherent pumping of a two-level system saturates at N1 = N2). The takeaway's 'every extra pumped atom adds a photon' is the ideal case: non-radiative decay and pump-to-upper-level efficiency lower it, and only the mirror-transmitted fraction leaves. Softened accordingly.

title: Dissolving: where does the sugar go?
interaction: Two glasses of water drawn as particles, one for sugar and one for salt, and a spoonful counter under each. One control at a time: tip in another spoonful, then slide the thermometer to warm both glasses. Each grain breaks into particles that wander off among the water particles until the water will take no more, and the rest sits on the bottom. Warming lets the sugar glass take spoonful after spoonful more, while the salt glass hardly takes any extra. At the end, let the water dry away and watch the same particles gather back into grains.
takeaway: Dissolved sugar and salt have not vanished: their particles are spread among the water's, each glass of water takes only so much, and warming lets it take far more sugar but hardly any more salt.
needs: Solubility of sucrose and of sodium chloride in water from 0 to 100 °C (about a dozen values) from the IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series, freely readable at NIST, or the ACS Middle School Chemistry tables; published facts, no dataset licence to clear.
needsSource: About a dozen tabulated solubility values (IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series via NIST; ACS Middle School Chemistry, chapter 5 lesson 6); facts, no licence needed.
pitfall: Dissolving is not melting, and the sugar does not disappear or turn into water: every particle is still there, which is why the water tastes sweet and weighs more. A full glass is not 'out of room' between water particles: it stops because dissolving and grains re-forming have come into balance.
why: England KS2 Year 5 'Properties and changes of materials' (dissolving; recovering a dissolved solid by evaporation): https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study; also NGSS 5-PS1-3 (solubility as an identifying property): https://www.nextgenscience.org/dci-arrangement/5-ps1-matter-and-its-interactions
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page changes the phase of one substance; this page mixes two solids into water and shows that temperature raises how much sugar water will take but barely changes salt. (The pool's dissolving-sugar was merged into this entry.)
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core KS2/KS3 idea (dissolving is not melting or vanishing, there is a limit, drying brings it back) with a clear particle mechanism no existing page shows; prerequisite for several other level-0 candidates.
build 4: The same honest particle model as dissolving-sugar, plus evaporation that recrystallises the solute, with a dozen handbook solubility values. Keep this one and fold dissolving-sugar into it.
verifyNote: It is distinct from the catalogue (states-of-matter changes one substance's phase), but it nearly duplicates the pool candidate dissolving-sugar: a particle counter, warming, a saturation limit, nothing lost. Its dry-it-back step overlaps separating-mixtures (the evaporating dish) and growing-crystals. The takeaway is also wrong for half the page. Salt's solubility barely changes with temperature (about 35.7 to 39 g per 100 g of water from 0 to 100 °C), while sucrose's rises from about 179 to 487 g. So 'warm water takes more' holds for sugar only. 'Until no more will fit' teaches the misconception that saturation means running out of room between water particles. The fix narrows the page to what neither sibling shows: sugar and salt side by side, and how differently temperature affects them. It should be merged with dissolving-sugar, or that one dropped.

title: Salt on ice: roads and ice cream
interaction: A block of ice drawn as a neat stack of water particles, with a thermometer. One control at a time: sprinkle salt, and salt particles get between the water particles at the surface so the stack cannot re-form, and the ice melts although the thermometer reads below freezing. Set the weather colder and the salt stops working; pour on more salt and see the point where extra salt no longer helps. Then put a bag of cream into the salted ice: the melting pulls heat out of the cream, the bath's thermometer drops below what plain ice could reach, and the cream freezes. Behind the picture runs the measured freezing-point curve of salt water and a running count of the heat that melting takes from the bath and the cream.
takeaway: Salt gets in the way of water re-freezing, so salted ice melts below freezing, and that melting draws so much heat out of its surroundings that a salt-and-ice bath gets colder than ice, cold enough to freeze cream.
needs: Freezing point of salt water against salt content (NaCl brine table and its lowest point, about minus 21 °C), from the US FHWA 'Manual of Practice for an Effective Anti-icing Program' (US government work, public domain).
needsSource: US FHWA brine freezing-point table, public domain US government work: https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/research/safety/95202/005.cfm
pitfall: Salt does not heat the ice or 'burn' through it, and it does not work at any cold: below about minus twenty, no amount of salt will melt ice.
why: Scientific American / Science Buddies 'Making Ice Cream in a Bag' (freezing-point depression for children): https://scientificamerican.com/article/scrumptious-science-making-ice-cream-in-a-bag/
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page melts a pure substance by raising its temperature; here the ice melts because of what is added to it, at a temperature where pure ice would stay solid.
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Salt blocking re-freezing and the ice-cream bath getting colder than ice is a surprising, distinct mechanism, though the heat-drawing half is hard to make honest for a 10-year-old without energy ideas.

build 4: Equilibrium on the NaCl brine liquidus (FHWA table, US government public domain) plus an energy balance for heat of fusion is an honest small model. The bath dropping below 0 °C and freezing the cream emerges from it.
verifyNote: No catalogue page covers freezing-point depression or freezing mixtures: states-of-matter covers only pure substances. Its level-0 framing works without formulas, using temperatures only as comparisons. The data source is real and public domain: FHWA-RD-95-202, Appendix B (freezing points of chemical solutions), is a US government work. The physics is right. NaCl brine's lowest freezing point is about −21 °C, the bath cools because melting absorbs heat, and the pitfall is correct. The one gap is that the interaction does not name its model. The honest model is the brine freezing-point curve plus a heat balance between ice, brine and cream, with the particle picture as illustration. A small edit makes that explicit and replaces the vague 'turn the cold down'.

title: Why metal feels cold
interaction: A table with a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a plastic cup and a woollen glove, all at room temperature, with a thermometer that reads the same on each. Drag a finger onto any one: a strip of heat colour flows out of the fingertip into the object, fast into the metal and barely at all into the wool, and a 'feels like' dial follows the temperature where skin meets object. One control: the room temperature. Warm the room past the temperature of your hand and the order flips, so the same metal now feels hottest. The flow is a heat-conduction model in which each material uses its real conductivity, density and heat capacity.
takeaway: Everything on the table is the same temperature; the metal feels cold because it draws heat out of your finger fastest, and when the room is warmer than your hand the same metal feels hottest.
needs: Thermal conductivity, density and specific heat of skin, a metal (steel or aluminium), wood, plastic and wool: under twenty published constants from textbook tables or Wikipedia's material-property tables (CC BY-SA). The model combines them, because contact temperature depends on all three.
needsSource: Under twenty published material constants (textbook tables; Wikipedia CC BY-SA); facts, no dataset
pitfall: Metal is not colder than wood, and cold does not flow into your hand: heat flows out of it, and a thermometer shows the two objects equal. The page also should not say conductivity alone decides it: how much heat the material soaks up per degree matters too.
why: Veritasium, 'Why Does Metal Feel Colder Than Wood If They're the Same Temperature?' (a classic misconception video): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vqDbMEdLiCs; England KS2 Year 5 lists thermal conductivity among material properties.
overlapWith: entropy: that page shows heat flowing between fast and slow particles at level 2; here it is one finger on one object, and the only question is how fast heat leaves the skin.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: It fixes a misconception everyone has with one finger, one control and a real conduction model, and no existing page covers it (it arguably belongs in physics rather than chemistry).

build 5: Two semi-infinite bodies in contact under 1D heat conduction, with real conductivity, density and heat capacity (thermal effusivity), give the contact temperature exactly at interactive rates from under ten public constants, and the result shows in the graphic.
verifyNote: It is distinct from entropy, levelled honestly for KS2 (Year 5 lists thermal conductivity among material properties), and buildable as 1D heat conduction between skin and object. The physics, though, is stated wrongly in two places. First, what sets the felt temperature is the contact temperature, which depends on each material's thermal effusivity sqrt(k·ρ·c) (conductivity, density and heat capacity together), not on conductivity alone. Physics-teaching papers flag 'conducts heat away faster' as the misleading version, so the model must use effusivity, even though the page never says the word. Second, metal feels hottest only when the room is warmer than the skin (above about 33 °C), not merely 'hot'.

title: Chromatography: separating by stickiness
interaction: Inject a mixture at the top of a column and watch each molecule hop at random between the moving phase and the stationary phase. The time each one spends stuck is set by its partition coefficient, so the bands separate and broaden, and a detector at the end draws the chromatogram. Slide the flow rate and the measured plate height traces the van Deemter curve: diffusion along the column dominates at slow flow, slow exchange at fast flow, and the uneven paths through the packing add a floor that the flow does not change. Lengthen the column or use finer packing to see the resolution improve.
takeaway: A column separates molecules by how much of the time each spends stuck rather than moving, and there is a best flow speed: slower and diffusion blurs the bands, faster and the molecules cannot keep up with the exchange.
pitfall: Most chromatography is not a sieve by size: two molecules of the same size separate because they stick differently. The bands are close to Gaussian only because each molecule makes many random hops that add up; with few exchanges or uneven sticky sites, real peaks tail.
why: Undergraduate analytical chemistry teaches band broadening through the van Deemter equation (Bates College chromatography learning objectives): https://www.bates.edu/chemistry-biochemistry/files/2012/01/wenzel-chrom-learning-objectives.pdf
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem: that page shows why sums of random steps are Gaussian; this one uses that fact to separate molecules and to find the flow rate that separates them best.
needsSource: none: the Giddings-Eyring stochastic model with illustrative partition coefficients and diffusivities, not values for named compounds
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Random partitioning that separates bands, plus the van Deemter optimum, is a real stochastic model a chemistry student learns, and no existing page covers it.

build 5: A random walk of molecules hopping between mobile and stationary phases by partition coefficient, with path-length and diffusion noise, separates and broadens bands and produces the van Deemter minimum from a sweep, with no data needed.
verifyNote: Distinct: no catalogue page covers separation or partitioning. central-limit-theorem only shows that sums of random steps are Gaussian, and reaction-rates-equilibrium shows forward and reverse rates, not differential migration or band broadening. Level 3 is honest because van Deemter plate height and resolution are taught in undergraduate analytical and instrumental chemistry (Bates, UML and UF lecture notes; LibreTexts CHM 331 problems). Both prerequisites are level 2, so neither sits above the topic. It is buildable as a real client-side model: the Giddings-Eyring stochastic model has particles hopping between the phases with exponential residence times set by k', plus axial diffusion and multipath, and runs easily at interactive rates. H(u) can be measured from the simulated peak variance and checked against H = A + B/u + Cu. It needs no external data: partition coefficients and diffusivities are generic parameters, not claims about real compounds. Two small accuracy fixes. First, the interaction says eddy paths, longitudinal diffusion and slow exchange 'each take their turn' as the flow changes. In the van Deemter equation the eddy (A) term does not depend on flow; it is a floor set by the packing. Only B/u dominates at low flow and Cu at high flow. Second, the pitfall says the bands are Gaussian because the hopping is random. They are only near-Gaussian, because many random hops add up; real peaks tail, and few exchanges or a heterogeneous surface skew them.

title: Dislocations: why metals bend and alloys resist
interaction: Shear a two-dimensional crystal of simulated atoms that contains an edge dislocation, and watch the defect glide one row of bonds at a time while a gauge shows the stress it took. Remove the dislocation, and the perfect crystal holds to a far higher stress before a whole plane slips at once. Sprinkle in larger or smaller foreign atoms and the dislocation snags on them, so the gauge must climb higher before it moves. Add a second and third dislocation and drive them against a row of obstacles, where they pile up and resist further slip.
takeaway: A crystal with a dislocation yields at a small fraction of the stress a perfect crystal needs, because the defect breaks one row of bonds at a time, and foreign atoms raise that stress by pinning it.
pitfall: Crystals do not deform by whole planes sliding at once; the theoretical strength computed that way is a thousand times higher than what any real metal shows.
why: MITx 3.012S.3x Structure of Materials covers dislocation descriptors and motion: https://openlearninglibrary.mit.edu/courses/course-v1:MITx+3.012S.3x+1T2019/about
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page colors members by stress; this one goes inside the metal to the defect that lets it yield and the atoms that stop it.
needsSource: none: a 2D Lennard-Jones crystal, the same kind of model states-of-matter runs; the ideal-against-measured shear strength factor is quoted from textbook values
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Why metals yield far below bond strength is a striking, showable mechanism at the heart of materials science, and no existing page covers it.

build 4: 2D Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics of a few thousand atoms with an edge dislocation glides under shear at interactive rates and shows solute pinning, but convincing work-hardening pile-ups need more atoms than a browser box holds, so that last step should stay modest.
verifyNote: Nothing in the catalogue covers dislocations (bridges-structures stays at the scale of members). Level 3 is honest: dislocation glide and solid-solution strengthening are core university materials science (MIT 3.012, MITx 3.012S.3x). A 2D Lennard-Jones crystal of a few hundred to a few thousand atoms is buildable on the client: states-of-matter already runs 2D molecular dynamics, and Bailey, Sethna and Myers simulate an edge dislocation in a 2D Lennard-Jones crystal. Three problems need fixing. (a) The takeaway's 'a thousand times below' cannot be observed in the graphic: a small 2D Lennard-Jones toy shows a large gap, but not the factor of 100 to 10,000 of real metals. The number belongs in the text, not the takeaway. (b) Work hardening by multiplying dislocations needs dislocation sources and large boxes; the honest small-box version is a pile-up against an obstacle. (c) newtons-laws is an unhelpful prerequisite. The crystal lattice comes from semiconductors ('Crystals & semiconductors') and the atom-box simulation from states-of-matter.

title: Molecular orbitals & conjugation
interaction: Snap carbon atoms into chains and rings to build a π system (ethene, butadiene, benzene, cyclobutadiene, the cyclopentadienyl anion, a cyanine dye); the page diagonalizes the Hückel matrix and draws the molecular orbitals as signed lobes on the atoms beside an energy ladder filled with the π electrons. Lengthen a cyanine chain and watch the HOMO-LUMO gap shrink beside the dye series' measured absorption maxima and a swatch of the colour it absorbs; close a chain into a ring and add or remove electrons to see which counts fill a closed shell and which leave two electrons alone in a degenerate pair.
takeaway: Electrons delocalized over a π system fill a ladder of orbitals whose gap narrows as the system grows, which is why longer dyes absorb redder light, and a ring is stabilized only when its π electrons exactly fill a closed shell (2, 6, 10: benzene) and destabilized when they half-fill a degenerate pair (4, 8: cyclobutadiene).
needs: Measured absorption maxima of a cyanine dye series for the color panel, to set beside the computed gap.
pitfall: Benzene's bonds do not alternate between single and double; the orbitals spread over the whole ring, and the two Kekulé drawings are a convention, not structures it flips between.
why: MIT OCW 5.61 Physical Chemistry devotes Lecture 26 to qualitative MO theory (Hückel): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/resources/qualitative-mo-theory-huckel/
overlapWith: chemical-bonds: that page builds molecules from localized electron pairs and VSEPR shapes; this one computes delocalized orbital energies and shapes from the Hückel Hamiltonian.
needsSource: Published λmax values of the classic cyanine dye series (literature numbers, not a licensed dataset); the Hückel model itself needs no data.
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Diagonalizing Hückel matrices to explain dye colour and aromaticity is a real model with a visual payoff, and chemical-bonds' VSEPR picture does not cover it.

build 5: Diagonalizing a small Hückel adjacency matrix is exact and instant, the ring and chain level patterns and aromaticity show directly, and the cyanine absorption maxima are published facts; simple Hückel gets only the trend of the gap, not absolute colours, and the page should say so.
verifyNote: Distinct: chemical-bonds (L1) uses localized pairs and VSEPR, and the pool's hartree-fock does a different self-consistent method. The level is honest (MIT 5.61 lecture on Hückel), the build is real (diagonalize an N×N matrix of at most about 20 sites in the browser), and the data are just literature λmax facts for a cyanine series, as used in standard undergraduate labs (KIT practical, Rioux). Two small faults. The takeaway ties stability to ring size ('six-membered stable, four-membered not'), but the actual rule is the electron count (4n+2 against 4n): cyclooctatetraene fails too, and charged rings such as C5H5- and C7H7+ pass. The interaction should also say that simple Hückel overestimates how far a polyene's gap closes, which is why the colour panel uses cyanines (bonds evened out) and not long polyenes.

title: Catalysis on a surface
interaction: Run CO oxidation on a lattice of catalyst sites: CO lands on one empty site, O2 splits onto two neighbouring empty sites, and adjacent CO and O react into CO2 and leave (the Ziff-Gulari-Barshad model). Slide the CO fraction in the gas: with too little CO the surface fills with oxygen and goes dead, across a narrow window the CO2 rate climbs, and just past its peak it collapses abruptly as CO covers every site, with the lattice's rate and coverages plotted beside the smooth mean-field Langmuir-Hinshelwood prediction that misses both dead ends. Add a CO desorption rate (a hotter surface) and watch the abrupt collapse soften and the poisoned surface recover.
takeaway: A catalyst works by holding the reactants next to each other on its surface, and too much of one reactant can cover every site and stop the reaction entirely.
pitfall: A catalyst is not consumed, but it is not inert either: its activity depends on what covers it, and a poisoned surface is a catalyst that has stopped working.
why: MIT OCW 10.37 Chemical and Biological Reaction Engineering covers heterogeneous catalysis and Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-37-chemical-and-biological-reaction-engineering-spring-2007/pages/lecture-notes
overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page's catalyst only lowers a barrier; this one models the surface sites, their coverage and the poisoning that follows.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The Ziff-Gulari-Barshad lattice model shows site coverage and CO poisoning, a mechanism the existing page's barrier-lowering catalyst never models.

build 5: The Ziff-Gulari-Barshad lattice model is a classic, cheap cellular simulation whose CO-poisoning transition emerges on its own, and adding desorption with temperature is a one-line extension. It needs no data.
verifyNote: Distinct from reaction-rates-equilibrium, whose catalyst only lowers a barrier, and a ZGB lattice Monte Carlo of about 100x100 sites runs easily in the browser; it needs no data. But the interaction misdescribes the ZGB model. The rate does not simply 'rise, peak and collapse as the surface smothers in CO'. Below a CO fraction of about 0.39 the surface is poisoned by oxygen (a continuous transition, rate zero), and the rate climbs across a reactive window before falling abruptly, a first-order jump, to CO poisoning at about 0.525. The 'Langmuir isotherm' alongside is also the wrong comparison: ZGB is a non-equilibrium steady state, so the fair comparison is the mean-field Langmuir-Hinshelwood rate, which misses the poisoning transitions the lattice shows. Small fix to the interaction; the takeaway already allows either reactant to poison.

title: Reaction trajectories & the transition state
interaction: Fire a quasiclassical trajectory of A + BC → AB + C across a potential-energy surface (LEPS model of H + H2 and F + H2) drawn as a contour map, choosing how much energy goes into translation and how much into vibration (never less than the zero-point vibration), and see whether it crosses the saddle or turns back. Compare the early barrier of F + H2 with the late barrier of its reverse, H + HF, to see that translation carries molecules over an early pass and vibration over a late one; sweep the temperature to watch the Eyring rate climb, and swap H for D to watch the zero-point energies, the effective barrier and the rate change.
takeaway: A reaction is a journey over a mountain pass on an energy landscape; the pass's height sets how often molecules make it and its position sets which kind of energy gets them over.
needs: LEPS (Sato) parameters for the H3 and FH2 surfaces.
pitfall: The transition state is not an intermediate that can be isolated; it is the top of the pass, crossed in a single vibration, and a catalyst lowers the pass rather than pushing molecules over it.
why: MIT OCW 5.60 covers rates of chemical reactions and transition-state theory (Lectures 33-35): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008/resources/lec33_th
overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page draws a 1D energy profile beside colliding balls; this one computes the 2D surface and real trajectories over it, with the isotope effect as a bonus.
needsSource: Published LEPS/Sato parameters for H + H2 and F + H2 (journal numbers; no licensed dataset).
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Classical trajectories on a LEPS surface with Polanyi's early/late barrier rules and the kinetic isotope effect are the real university model behind the 1D profile on reaction-rates-equilibrium.

build 5: Classical trajectories on a LEPS surface for H+H2 and F+H2 are a textbook small ODE with published Sato parameters (facts). Polanyi's early/late barrier rules and Eyring rates follow directly. The zero-point-energy isotope effect must be added as a stated harmonic correction.
verifyNote: Distinct from reaction-rates-equilibrium (a 1D profile only), and buildable: collinear A+BC on a LEPS surface is a 2-degree-of-freedom ODE, cheap to integrate live, and LEPS/Sato parameters for H3 and FH2 are published numbers reproduced in teaching labs (for example the Imperial College MRD lab). The level is honest (MIT 5.60). But a purely classical trajectory has no zero-point energy, so the H/D swap as written cannot show a ZPE effect. The trajectories must be quasiclassical (the initial vibration seeded with its ZPE) and the Eyring rate must use a ZPE-corrected barrier, and even then the transition state's ZPE is a known weakness of QCT. 'Move the barrier early or late' also has no honest continuous control on a fixed LEPS surface. The honest version is to compare F+H2 (early barrier), its reverse H+HF (late barrier) and symmetric H+H2.

title: How ants find the shortest way
interaction: Ants wander out of a nest at random; one that finds the sugar walks home laying a scent, and the others tend to follow scent, so a trail forms and thickens. Drag the sugar farther away or drop a pebble on the trail and watch the colony reroute. Then offer a long bridge and a short one together and count the ants on each: ants on the short one get back first, so its scent builds up sooner and the short one wins. Open the short bridge only after a trail has formed on the long one, and the colony stays on the long one until the scent's fading is switched on.
takeaway: A colony finds the shorter path with no map and no ant that knows it: ants on the short route return sooner, so its scent builds up faster and draws more ants, and a fading scent lets the colony give up an old route.
pitfall: No ant knows where the food is or compares the routes, and the queen gives no orders. Fading is not what makes the short bridge win when both are offered at once; it is what lets a colony switch to a shortcut that appears later, and real Argentine ants often do not. Real ants also use sight and memory, which the page leaves out and says so.
why: The NetLogo Ants model, a standard classroom agent model of pheromone trails (Deneubourg's double-bridge experiment): https://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/Ants
overlapWith: graph-search: an algorithm explores a map systematically to find the shortest route; this page finds one with many simple agents and a fading scent, with no map at all.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Stigmergy with fading pheromone is a clear emergent mechanism a 10-year-old can run and test (double bridge, evaporation off), and nothing on the site shows it.

build 5: A pheromone-laying and evaporating agent model with the double-bridge experiment is a classic, cheap simulation whose takeaway emerges visibly (shorter bridge wins; no evaporation means lock-in). It needs no data.
verifyNote: Distinct from graph-search (no map, agents plus a scent field), honest level 0, and buildable as an agent model with a pheromone grid (NetLogo Ants). The problem is the mechanism. In Deneubourg's and Goss's double-bridge work the short branch wins because ants that take it get back sooner and lay scent on it first, so it pulls ahead even with no fading. Fading matters when a shortcut appears later: Goss et al. 1989 (Naturwissenschaften 76:579) added the short branch after a trail had formed, and the Argentine ants mostly stayed on the long one. So 'with fading switched off the colony stays stuck on whichever bridge it found first' is wrong when both bridges are offered at once, and the takeaway credits the fading for what the round-trip time does. The fix rewrites the interaction and takeaway to separate the two effects.

title: Camouflage: you are the hungry bird
interaction: Moths of many shades rest on a tree trunk and the reader is the bird: tap every moth you spot before the timer runs out. The survivors lay eggs that look like their parents, give or take a little, and the next generation appears; after a few rounds the reader flips the bark from pale to sooty and keeps hunting.
takeaway: The moths you fail to see are the ones that have babies, so after a few generations the moths match the bark, and when the bark changes, so do the moths.
needs: Bark textures, either procedurally generated or public-domain or CC0 photographs from Wikimedia Commons; the moth population model needs no data.
pitfall: A moth does not change colour to hide, and no moth chooses its colour; the population changes because the visible ones are eaten before they breed.
why: England national curriculum, KS2 Year 6 'Evolution and inheritance': identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment and that adaptation may lead to evolution (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); NGSS MS-LS4-4 (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ls4-4-biological-evolution-unity-and-diversity).
overlapWith: evolution: that page runs a population with sliders for mutation, population size and environment; here the reader is the predator, and the selection is their own clicking, which is the level-0 doorway into that page.
needsSource: none, or CC0/public-domain bark photographs (Wikimedia Commons)
verifyNote: Sound in substance. The model (heritable shade with small variation, plus the reader's own predation) is real and cheap. The takeaway shows in the graphic, and the pitfall is right. The page differs from evolution, where the predator is a slider, because here the reader is the predator. leadsTo evolution and meiosis-inheritance are both existing level-1 pages. The weak point is the 'why': a CliffsNotes page is not a curriculum source. The KS2 Year 6 statutory requirement on adaptation and the NGSS standard should be cited directly.
judgeNotes: build 4: The heritable-shade population model with the reader as selective predator is a real, simple genetic model rather than a picture to tap, since the next generation is computed from the survivors; procedural bark avoids licence questions.
fit-level 5: The reader acting as the selective predator makes the mechanism the toy itself, a strong level-0 doorway to evolution that is distinct from that page's slider-driven population.

title: Fireflies that flash together
interaction: A meadow of fireflies, each with its own inner clock that flashes when it strikes twelve and starts again. One control: how much a neighbour's flash nudges a firefly's clock forward. At zero the meadow twinkles at random; turn it up and patches start flashing together, then waves, then the whole field as one; drag a finger through the swarm to scramble it and watch it fall back into step.
takeaway: Thousands of fireflies flash together with no conductor, because each one nudges its own clock a little toward every flash it sees.
pitfall: There is no lead firefly and no outside signal; synchrony appears only from each insect reacting to its neighbours. Only some firefly species do this.
why: Nicky Case's 'Fireflies' explorable (public domain), the interactive credited in Veritasium's synchronization video: https://ncase.me/fireflies/
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: one oscillator pushed at a frequency; this page is many self-timed flashers nudging each other into step, which is not resonance. The runner-up kuramoto-synchronization (level 3) is the grown-up phase-coupled model.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Pulse-coupled oscillators syncing with one coupling slider is a magical, genuinely model-driven level-0 toy, distinct from resonance and from the flocking and ant emergence pages.
build 5: Mirollo-Strogatz pulse-coupled integrate-and-fire oscillators on a 2D field are cheap and honest, and synchrony visibly emerges as the single coupling slider rises. It needs no data.
verifyNote: No existing page shows pulse-coupled synchronization. oscillations-resonance is one driven oscillator, and the pool's kuramoto-synchronization is the level-3 phase model, so this is the level-0 entry to it. The model is a pulse-coupled integrate-and-fire population (Mirollo-Strogatz, as in Nicky Case's explorable), which runs easily in the browser with one coupling control, and the synchrony is visible without text. Needs no data. The takeaway and pitfall are sound: there is no leader, and only some species (Photinus carolinus, Pteroptyx) do this. The leadsTo link to oscillations-resonance is loose but acceptable.

title: Flocks without a leader
interaction: A hundred birds fly across the stage following three rules, each drawn as a short arrow on one highlighted bird: keep a little distance from your neighbours, fly the way they fly, drift toward the middle of them. Switch one rule off at a time: without the first the birds pile into clumps, without the second the flock never agrees on a direction, without the third it scatters. Add a hawk and watch the flock split around it and close again with no bird in charge.
takeaway: A flock can hold together and turn as one with no leader: in the model, three simple rules about each bird's nearest neighbours are enough to make one.
pitfall: No bird leads or sees the whole flock, and the three rules are a model that reproduces flocking, not a list real birds were found to obey. Real starlings each keep track of about six or seven nearest neighbours, however far apart they are (Ballerini et al. 2008), and nobody plans the shapes of a murmuration.
why: NGSS 3-LS2-1 (some animals form groups that help members survive); Reynolds's boids is the classic classroom model of it (MIT StarLogo activity): https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ls2-1-ecosystems-interactions-energy-and-dynamics
overlapWith: ecosystems: populations tied together by birth and predation rates; this page is the movement of one group where each animal follows a rule about its neighbours, with no population counts at all.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Boids' three rules, switched off one at a time, is the canonical emergent-behaviour toy, wordless and formula-free, with no counterpart on the site.
build 5: Reynolds boids with switchable separation/alignment/cohesion rules and a predator is a classic, small agent simulation in which each rule's effect is directly observable. It needs no data.
verifyNote: Distinct from ecosystems (population counts, not movement) and buildable: boids run in the browser at interactive rates, at an honest level 0, with NGSS 3-LS2-1 as the signal. The fault is factual. The takeaway says real flocks keep their shape 'because every bird follows the same three simple rules'. Reynolds's three rules are a model that reproduces flocking, not measured bird behaviour. Field data (Ballerini et al. 2008, PNAS) show starlings each track a fixed count of about six or seven nearest neighbours, whatever the distance. The takeaway should say the rules are sufficient, not that they are what birds do, and the pitfall can name the measured neighbour count.

title: Diffusion, osmosis & active transport
interaction: Drop dye into one corner of a box of jiggling particles and watch it spread, faster when warmer, while a concentration graph flattens. Put a membrane down the middle with pores that pass water but not sugar, set the sugar concentration on each side and watch the water level rise on the sugary side; then make the box a cell, place it in pure water, salt water and something in between, and see it swell, shrink or hold, as a potato slice does in the classroom experiment. Finally switch on a pump that carries particles against the gradient and watch its ATP meter drain.
takeaway: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are not by random motion alone; a membrane that holds dissolved particles back makes water flow toward the side with more of them; and moving anything the other way costs energy.
needsSource: none
pitfall: Osmosis moves water toward the side with more dissolved particles, but not because those particles 'dilute' the water so that fewer water molecules reach the pore: the flow is far larger than water's own diffusion would give, and it comes from the trapped particles pushing on the membrane. Diffusion needs no force or pump; particles have no direction of their own, and the net flow is a counting effect. A plant cell in pure water becomes firm rather than bursting, because of its wall.
why: AQA GCSE Biology 8461 topic 4.1.3 'Transport in cells' (diffusion, osmosis, active transport) with Required practical 3, osmosis in plant tissue https://www.edplace.com/gcse-revision/biology/aqa
overlapWith: entropy (level 2) shows two gases mixing as a count of microstates and the-cell shows the membrane as a structure; neither has a membrane that passes water and holds solute, a cell that swells or shrinks, or a pump that spends ATP. The pool's smells-and-diffusion (level 0) spreads a smell without the membrane.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core GCSE topic missing from the catalogue, with particle-level mechanisms the graphic shows naturally (spreading, membrane, swelling cell, pump); entropy's mixing count and the-cell's structure do not cover it.

build 4: A 2D particle box with a membrane that passes only solvent particles is a real model and close to the existing states-of-matter engine; diffusion, osmotic flow and a pump that spends ATP all come out of it, though the scope (four scenes) is large, and in 2D the water level has to be shown as a movable partition or the compartment's volume, not as true hydrostatic height.
verifyNote: Distinct enough: entropy mixes two gases with no membrane, the-cell is structure, and the pool's level-0 smells-and-diffusion has no membrane, no osmosis and no pump. The level-1 rating is honest (AQA GCSE 4.1.3), the prerequisites are level 1, and a particle box with a membrane that lets water through and blocks solute is a real client-side model. The flaw is that the takeaway says water 'does the same' as diffusing particles, the textbook story that water flows down its own concentration gradient. That is a known misconception: Kramer and Myers (2013, Trends in Plant Science) show osmotic flow is several times larger than water's diffusion alone would give, and it comes from the solute's push on the membrane. The particle simulation would itself show bulk flow, so the page must not explain it as dilution. The fix keeps the GCSE outcome (water moves toward the side with more dissolved particles) without the false cause.

title: PCR: copying DNA until there is enough to see
interaction: A tube with a few strands of DNA and a thermometer: step through one cycle (heat to split the strands, cool so short primers stick at the ends of the target, warm for the enzyme to extend them) and two strands become four; press play and the count doubles every cycle while the plot shoots up and the primers and building blocks run down. Set the starting number of copies and see when the glowing signal crosses the detection line: one copy takes about ten cycles longer than a thousand, which is how a PCR test reads how much virus was in the swab. Change the primers and a non-matching DNA stays uncopied.
takeaway: PCR copies a chosen stretch of DNA by doubling it every heating-and-cooling cycle, so thirty cycles turn a few molecules into a billion, and the cycle at which the signal appears says how many there were to start with.
pitfall: Doubling is not forever: primers and nucleotides run out and the curve flattens, so the plateau says nothing about the starting amount; only the threshold cycle does. A Ct value is not a measure of how ill someone is. Nor is every copy the target from the first cycle: the short piece bounded by both primers only appears from the third cycle, after which it dominates.
why: 'How does a PCR test work' became a mass question in 2020; public-health explainer of cycles and Ct values: https://www.publichealthontario.ca/en/About/News/2021/Explained-COVID19-PCR-Testing-and-Cycle-Thresholds
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: how DNA is read into protein; this page is how a chosen piece of DNA is copied in a tube and counted. dna-sequencing (pool, level 3) reads the letters; PCR only multiplies a chosen piece.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Its doubling-per-cycle model and the Ct readout are a vivid, real mechanism that everyone met through COVID tests, and it is distinct from dna-to-protein; the PCR-test link fits level 1 well.

build 5: Doubling per cycle, with efficiency falling as primers and nucleotides run out, is a small exact model; the threshold-cycle shift of log2(1000), about ten cycles, comes straight out of it, and primer matching is a simple string test.
verifyNote: Distinct from every existing page: dna-to-protein reads a gene, and nothing in the catalogue covers amplification. The pool's dna-fingerprinting uses PCR only as one step. The model (doubling per cycle, logistic depletion of primers and nucleotides, threshold crossing) is small and real. The quoted numbers check out: at 100% efficiency each tenfold dilution adds about 3.32 cycles, so 1 copy versus 1000 copies is about 10 cycles, and 2^30 is about 1e9. The pitfall is sound: the plateau carries no information about the starting amount, and Ct tracks the amount of template, not how ill someone is. Level 1 is honest (A-level and IB biology teach PCR, and the doubling arithmetic is high-school level). No external data is needed. Small fix: the exact target-length fragment only appears from cycle 3, so the page should not draw the first doublings as already target-sized copies.

title: Bacterial chemotaxis
interaction: Release a few hundred E. coli into a dish with a drop of attractant and watch each one run straight, tumble, and run again; inside each cell a Barkai-Leibler receptor model sets the tumble rate, and the swarm drifts up the gradient. Move the drop, flood the dish with a uniform dose and watch the tumble rate dip then recover exactly (perfect adaptation), and change the adaptation time or the swim speed to see the biased random walk fail.
takeaway: A bacterium is too small to sense a gradient across its body, so it compares now with a moment ago and tumbles less when things are getting better; that biased random walk is enough to climb a gradient.
pitfall: The cell does not steer toward the attractant: it cannot tell direction, it only changes how often it tumbles, and the page must not draw it turning toward the source.
why: CourseSource lesson on building and simulating a chemotaxis model in Cell Collective (QUBES): https://qubeshub.org/publications/5179/

title: Morphogen gradients & positional information
interaction: Drag the production rate, diffusion constant and lifetime of a morphogen made at one end of a row of cells and watch its concentration profile settle into an exponential whose length scale, the square root of diffusion over decay, the page reports. Double the tissue's length and the bands fail to scale; switch on Ben-Zvi and Barkai's expansion-repression circuit (a second diffusing 'expander' that widens the gradient and is shut off by the morphogen) and the bands stay in proportion. Add noise to the concentration and see that boundaries where the gradient is steep stay sharp while those in its flat tail blur.
takeaway: A cell can learn where it is from how much of one substance reaches it, and the shape of that gradient, set by diffusion and decay, decides where the boundaries fall.

pitfall: The synthesis-diffusion-degradation model is a working hypothesis and the Bicoid gradient's formation is still debated; the page must present the exponential as what the model predicts and say where it is tested.
why: Stanford course on morphogenesis listing morphogen gradients and Turing patterns: https://bulletin.stanford.edu/courses/2126934

needsSource: none (model only; quoted literature values cited, not redistributed)

title: Population genetics: drift & selection
interaction: Run a hundred Wright-Fisher populations at once as allele-frequency traces: with no selection they wander and fix at random, faster in small populations; with a selection coefficient s they bend toward fixation, and a counter shows the share of new beneficial mutations that fix, approaching Haldane's 2s however large the population, so most are lost anyway. Set dominance to see recessive alleles hide from selection, and compare the Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies with the simulated ones each generation.
takeaway: Allele frequencies change by chance as well as by selection: in a small population chance can fix a harmful allele or lose a good one, and even in a large population most new beneficial mutations vanish while they are still rare.
pitfall: Hardy-Weinberg is not 'evolution stops': it is the one-generation baseline that shows which forces are absent, and drift is not selection by another name; the page must keep them separate.
why: Cal State LA BIOL 415 Population Genetics syllabus (Hardy-Weinberg, drift, effective size, selection, coalescent): https://www.calstatela.edu/sites/default/files/syllabibiol415.pdf
overlapWith: evolution: that page shifts a trait distribution with predators and food; this one tracks a single allele's frequency and separates chance from selection with explicit N and s.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Wright-Fisher drift versus selection, with Kimura's fixation probability, is the core university model the evolution page lacks, and it is ideal for many live traces.
build 5: A hundred Wright-Fisher binomial traces per generation are cheap, and fixation near 2s and the Hardy-Weinberg ratios are exact checks; no data needed.
verifyNote: The topic is distinct from evolution (an explicit allele with N and s, and drift kept apart from selection). The Wright-Fisher model is binomial sampling, trivially fast for a hundred populations, and level 3 is honest (university population genetics, per the cited syllabus). It has two factual errors. (1) The interaction says the counter shows how often a beneficial mutation is lost, 'approaching Kimura's 2s', but 2s is the probability of fixation, not of loss (Haldane 1927, generalized by Kimura). (2) The takeaway says most beneficial mutations are lost because the population is small, but a new beneficial mutation fixes with probability about 2s whatever N is (once Ns >> 1), so even in a huge population most are lost by chance while still rare. Small N makes drift dominate selection: that is the regime where |Ns| is about 1 or less.

title: Turing patterns
interaction: Run an activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion system on a grid from near-uniform noise and watch spots or stripes crystallise. Change the ratio of the two diffusion rates and the pattern appears only once the inhibitor spreads much faster than the activator; change the reaction rates to move from spots to stripes to labyrinths; grow the domain and extra stripes insert themselves, and taper the grid into a tail to see spots become bands as it narrows.
takeaway: Two chemicals, one that makes more of itself and a faster-spreading one that suppresses it, can turn a uniform field into regular spots or stripes with no blueprint, at a spacing set by their reaction and diffusion rates.
pitfall: Not every stripe in nature is a Turing pattern. The page should name where a Turing-type mechanism is well supported (digit spacing, hair and feather follicles) and where the evidence is mixed (fish skin, where pigment cells also move). It must not claim the mechanism for zebra stripes or fingerprints without saying that is contested.
why: University of Manchester undergraduate brochure feature on the Turing pattern: https://www.scieng.manchester.ac.uk/undergraduate-brochures/2024/the-turing-pattern/
overlapWith: chaos-fractals: that page grows patterns by iterating a map; here they grow from a PDE with a definite wavelength, and the control is the diffusion ratio.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Reaction-diffusion spots and stripes are a beautiful, widely sought mechanism driven by a real PDE, and they are distinct from chaos-fractals.

build 5: A Gierer-Meinhardt or Gray-Scott grid PDE runs at interactive rates in JS (or WebGL) and shows the diffusion-ratio threshold honestly; growing and tapered domains are a mask on the same grid.

Two small corrections. The wavelength is set by the reaction rates together with the two diffusion coefficients, not by 'rates alone'. The angelfish case is itself debated (Painter, Maini & Othmer 1999 add cell movement), so the pitfall should hedge it.

title: How your ear hears
interaction: Slide a tone from low to high and watch it shake the big eardrum, which passes the shake through three tiny bones onto a much smaller window into the fluid of the snail-shaped cochlea, concentrating the push; a ripple then runs along the cochlea's ribbon until it peaks at one spot. Each pitch peaks somewhere else, high notes near the entrance and low notes at the far end. Play two notes at once and see two bumps; turn the loudness up and the bumps grow.
takeaway: The ear sorts sounds by pitch before the brain hears them: each note makes a different place along the spiral wiggle.
needsSource: none: the Greenwood (1961) frequency-to-place function for the human cochlea, the middle ear's eardrum-to-footplate area ratio (about 17 to 1) with a small ossicle lever (about 1.3), and a passive bank of tuned filters for the ribbon, stated as a simplification
pitfall: The cochlea is not a microphone with one signal: it is thousands of sensors each listening at its own spot. Loud is not the same as high: loudness mainly grows the bump, pitch moves it. And the little bones are not the main amplifier: most of the boost comes from a big eardrum pushing on a tiny window.
why: NGSS MS-LS1-8: sensory receptors respond to stimuli, with ear receptors reacting to vibrations. https://nyssls.info/index.php/MS-LS1-8
overlapWith: waves-interference: that page is the wave in the air; this one is the receiver, from eardrum to the place-by-pitch map. The reserve item Hearing and the cochlea merges here at level 0; the cochlea's own mechanics (travelling wave, active amplifier) stay open for a level-3 page.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Promotes the reserve cochlea item as a clear place-by-pitch mechanism with one slider, distinct from waves-interference's wave in the air.

build 4: The Greenwood place function with a bank of passive resonators along the basilar membrane, driven by the tone, computes the bump positions honestly and runs easily; the ossicle lever is a stated gain.

'Three tiny bones lever the shake' and a needsSource of 'a middle-ear lever ratio' would teach the wrong thing. Also loudness does not only grow the bump: loud tones broaden it and shift it slightly, so the pitfall should say 'mainly'.

title: Muscles pull in pairs
interaction: Drag the hand of a cutaway arm: bending the elbow, the biceps shortens and bulges; straightening it against a push, such as pressing down on a table or pushing up from a chair, the triceps shortens instead, and tugging either muscle alone shows it can only pull, never push. Hang a bag of shopping from the hand and watch the biceps pull many times the bag's weight, because it grips the forearm so close to the elbow; lower the bag slowly and the biceps is still the one pulling, getting longer as it lets the bag down.
takeaway: A muscle can only pull, so every joint needs a pair that take turns, and the one that grips near the elbow must pull far harder than the weight in your hand.
needsSource: none: a two-link lever with real attachment distances (biceps a few centimetres from the elbow, the hand some thirty-five centimetres away) gives the force ratio

judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Antagonistic pairs plus the elbow lever (the biceps pulls many times the load) is a vivid mechanism readable with counts and comparisons only, and nothing existing shows it.

The page must show this or it repeats the error the pitfall claims to avoid.

title: Why spinning makes you dizzy
interaction: Spin a head on a chair with a slider and watch the fluid in the ear's three rings lag behind, bending the little flap that tells the brain turning; keep spinning at a steady speed and the fluid catches up, so the feeling fades. Stop suddenly and the fluid keeps going, the flap bends the other way, and the brain reports turning in the opposite direction while the room stands still: that is dizzy.
takeaway: Your ears sense turning with a ring of fluid, and when you stop spinning the fluid keeps going, so you feel you are turning the other way.
needsSource: none: the torsion-pendulum model of the semicircular canal (fluid lag with a time constant of a few seconds, plus the brain's longer velocity storage), driven by the slider's turning speed
pitfall: Dizziness after spinning is not blood sloshing or the brain being overwhelmed by speed: the sensor is faithfully reporting a real movement of fluid that is no longer the head's movement.

overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page drives a spring; this one is a sensor's lag, with the same inner ear as hearing-and-the-ear but a different organ in it.
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Lagging fluid in the semicircular canals, and the reversed feeling on stopping, is a clean inertia mechanism every child has felt, and no existing page covers it.

title: Why you get sleepy
interaction: Set a bedtime and a wake-up time and run three days: a sleep-pressure tank fills while you are awake and drains while you sleep, and a body clock sets the hours when sleep comes easily; sleepiness is the gap between them. Skip a night and watch the tank overflow; nap in the afternoon and see tonight's sleep come later. A strip under the plot sketches the night's usual rounds of light and deep sleep, about ninety minutes each.
takeaway: Sleepiness is a pressure that builds all day and drains at night, gated by a clock that opens a window for it; when the two disagree you lie awake tired or nod off at noon.
needsSource: none: the two-process model (Borbely 1982; retrospective at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9540767/) is an exponential sleep pressure and a daily rhythm with two thresholds; the night stages follow the standard ninety-minute cycle
pitfall: The page explains when you get sleepy, not why animals sleep at all, which is still an open question. And the body clock is not fixed: late mornings and evening screen light push it later, which is why a weekend of lie-ins makes Monday feel like jet lag (the toy keeps the clock fixed, and says so).
why: England statutory RSHE and health education guidance, primary health education: the importance of sufficient good quality sleep for health, the amount of sleep recommended for their age, and practical steps for improving sleep. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/relationships-education-relationships-and-sex-education-rse-and-health-education
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page is a feedback loop around blood sugar over hours; this one is a pressure and a clock over days, with no hormones shown.
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The two-process model (a sleep-pressure tank plus a circadian window) is a real model that works as a level-0 toy with one bedtime control, high in everyday interest and distinct from homeostasis.

build 5: Borbely's two-process model (exponential Process S, sinusoidal Process C, two thresholds) is a published, tiny model that runs instantly and shows sleep deprivation and nap effects without text; the ninety-minute stage strip is an honest stylisation.
verifyNote: Distinct and buildable (Borbely two-process model, no data needed; the L3 pool candidate circadian-clocks handles the gene loop), but the pitfall is factually wrong: a weekend lie-in does shift the clock, because late waking moves light exposure, meals and activity later and delays the circadian rhythm; that delay is what social jet lag is (Roenneberg). title: Pharmacokinetics & dosing
interaction: Place doses on a timeline from a palette (an injection, a tablet, a steady drip, a loading dose) and run them through a one-compartment model whose clearance, volume of distribution and absorption rate are sliders; the blood level is plotted against the drug's therapeutic window. title: The cerebellum & motor learning
interaction: Move the mouse or a finger to targets while the cursor is secretly rotated by thirty degrees, and watch yourself miss, correct and adapt over a few dozen reaches; beside the hand, a two-rate error-driven model (a fast and a slow learner) updates its prediction trial by trial and its curve sits over the reader's own. Remove the rotation and say 'aim straight': the aftereffect that remains is the implicit, cerebellar part. Reverse the rotation briefly, then hide the errors, and both the model and the hand drift back toward the first adaptation as the fast learner fades and the slow one remains.
takeaway: An implicit learner nudges its prediction a little after every miss, and the aftereffect that survives being told the world is back to normal shows a correction that was learned, not reasoned.
needsSource: none; the two-rate model is Smith, Ghazizadeh & Shadmehr, PLoS Biology 4(6): e179 (2006): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1463025

why: Motor adaptation and the cerebellum are standard neuroscience-course content and a high-traffic reference topic: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_learning

verifyNote: Distinct (no motor-learning page; reinforcement-learning and gradient-descent are different), buildable (the reader's own cursor reaches under a rotation, plus the Smith-Ghazizadeh-Shadmehr 2006 two-rate state-space model, open access), and honestly level 3.
