title: Hearing & the cochlea
interaction: Play a tone, a chord or a spoken word into a cochlea modelled as a chain of coupled resonators whose stiffness falls along the basilar membrane, and watch the travelling wave peak at a place that depends on frequency. Drag the frequency and the peak moves; switch on the outer hair cells' amplification and the peak sharpens; kill the outer hair cells at the place tuned near 4 kHz, as loud noise does, and the audiogram develops the classic notch. Then replace the cochlea with a cochlear implant: split the sound into a few bands, drive one electrode per band, and hear the result.
takeaway: The cochlea sorts sound by frequency along its length, so pitch is a place, and a cochlear implant works by stimulating those places with a handful of electrodes.
needs: A short openly licensed speech clip for the implant demonstration (a LibriSpeech utterance, CC BY 4.0, or synthesized speech); the cochlear model itself is a standard one-dimensional transmission-line model with published parameters.
needsSource: LibriSpeech, CC BY 4.0 (https://www.openslr.org/12), or speech synthesized in the browser; no other data
pitfall: Noise damage does not simply turn the volume down: the lost hair cells remove the amplification, so soft sounds vanish while loud ones still hurt.
why: MIT OCW HST.720 Physiology of the Ear covers cochlear mechanics and cochlear amplification as core sessions: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-720-physiology-of-the-ear-fall-2004/
overlapWith: vision-color: that page builds an image and colour from three kinds of sensor; this page builds pitch from thousands of sensors in a row, each tuned by its position.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The site has no hearing page; the place code (a travelling wave on a graded membrane) and the cochlear-implant finale make a strong, visual, distinct level-3 mechanism.

build 4: A frequency-domain 1D transmission-line cochlea and a band vocoder (Web Audio) for the implant are both cheap. The outer-hair-cell gain is a phenomenological negative damping and should be stated as one. A CC0 speech clip is easy to find.

title: The ECG & arrhythmias
interaction: Run a sheet of heart muscle as an excitable medium (the Aliev–Panfilov equations on a grid) with a pacemaker, a fast conduction path and a slow atrioventricular node, and read a pseudo-ECG off it: the tissue's net electrical vector projected onto the three limb leads of Einthoven's triangle. Then break it: slow conduction in a patch, add a scar, fire an early beat into tissue that has only partly recovered and watch a spiral wave take over the trace as tachycardia and then break up into fibrillation; deliver a shock that excites every cell at once and lets the pacemaker take back control. Real annotated recordings from the MIT-BIH database sit beside the simulated traces for comparison.
takeaway: An ECG is the shadow of a wave of excitation crossing the heart, and the most dangerous fast rhythms are usually not a faster pacemaker but a wave that finds a loop and chases its own tail.
needs: Annotated ECG records from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database on PhysioNet (Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0).
needsSource: PhysioNet MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, ODC-By 1.0: https://physionet.org/content/mitdb/1.0.0/
pitfall: A defibrillator does not restart a stopped heart: it stops a chaotic rhythm so the natural pacemaker can take over, and a flat line is not a shockable rhythm. And not every arrhythmia is re-entry: a heart can also beat too slowly when conduction is blocked.
why: Rhythm interpretation and the conduction system are Cardiovascular-system content in the USMLE Step 1 content outline: https://www.usmle.org/pdfs/step-1/content_step1.pdf
overlapWith: heart-circulation: that page shows a healthy ECG synchronized with the beating pump; this page computes the ECG from a model of the tissue and lets the reader break the rhythm.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Computing the ECG from an excitable-medium model and breaking it into a spiral wave goes far past heart-circulation's synced trace, and it is a showcase mechanism at an honest level 3.

build 4: Aliev–Panfilov on a grid of about 150 by 150 runs spiral waves at interactive rates, a dipole projection gives an honest ECG, and MIT-BIH is ODC-By (verified on PhysioNet). Putting a conduction system and AV node on a 2D sheet is a hand-built approximation and should be presented as one.
verifyNote: Distinct from heart-circulation, whose ECG is a drawn P-QRS-T template (circulation.ts) with no tissue model, re-entry or fibrillation. Level 3 is honest because cardiac excitable-media modelling is a biomedical-engineering topic, and all prerequisites are level 1 or 2. It is buildable: a 2D Aliev-Panfilov grid runs explicitly in the browser (an ibiblio e-notes HTML5 demo runs 512x512), and a ~150x150 grid with a pseudo-ECG computed from the dipole is light. The MIT-BIH data is confirmed as ODC-By 1.0 on PhysioNet. Two problems, both small. (1) The takeaway overstates: not every dangerous rhythm is re-entry. Complete heart block (too slow), triggered activity and torsades also exist, and some fast rhythms come from a focus that fires too often. (2) The interaction implies real limb leads from a whole heart. A 2D sheet gives a pseudo-ECG from the net dipole, so it should say so, so the reader doesn't take the simulated trace for a clinical 12-lead. The pitfall is correct.

title: MRI: an image from spinning protons
interaction: Start where Medical imaging stops: one gradient turns position into frequency. Step through a real 2D pulse sequence on a phantom: a slice-selective pulse tips the protons, a phase-encoding gradient gives each row its own twist, and a readout gradient records one line of the slice's 2D Fourier transform. Watch k-space fill line by line beside the image that its inverse transform gives so far. A Bloch-equation view of a few spins shows them fan out and refocus into an echo. Then edit k-space: keep only the centre for a blurred image, only the edges for outlines, skip every other line to fold the image onto itself, or shrink the field of view until the head wraps around.
takeaway: An MRI scanner never measures a picture: gradients give each position its own precession frequency and phase, so every echo is one line of the image's 2D Fourier transform, and the centre of k-space carries the contrast while its edges carry the detail.
needs: The Shepp-Logan phantom (a mathematical object, no data); optionally one real T1-weighted brain slice.
pitfall: MRI uses no ionizing radiation, and the image is not proton density alone. A point in k-space is not a pixel: every sample holds information about the whole image, which is why dropping lines blurs or ghosts the whole picture instead of leaving holes.
why: 'How does an MRI work' is among the most-asked medical-technology questions, and k-space MRI theory is a standard biomedical-engineering course (Purdue BME 55500): https://engineering.purdue.edu/online/courses/tagged_items/magnetic-resonance-imaging-mri-theory
overlapWith: medical-imaging: that page already shows Larmor precession, a single gradient whose Fourier transform gives a 1D water profile, and T1/T2 contrast from TR and TE; this page adds 2D phase-plus-frequency encoding, the echo, filling k-space line by line, and the artefacts of editing it. nmr-spectroscopy (pool, chemistry, level 3) has the same spins and pulses but no gradients and no image.
needsSource: Shepp-Logan: none. Real slice, if used: an OpenNeuro dataset (CC0), named on the page.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: medical-imaging only sketches MRI; the Bloch equations, the gradients and filling k-space make a distinct, visually striking level-3 page built on fourier-transform.

build 5: Bloch precession for the signal and a 2D FFT of an analytic Shepp–Logan phantom (line-by-line k-space filling and masking) are small, exact and fast; OpenNeuro data are CC0 if a real slice is wanted.
verifyNote: Partly duplicated, and the overlapWith is inaccurate. medical-imaging does not just sketch MRI at the end. It has three full MRI steps (src/routes/medical-imaging/steps.ts): Larmor precession; a gradient whose received signal is Fourier-transformed into a water profile (gradientEcho in imaging.ts, which is exactly 'the signal is the image's Fourier transform' in 1D); and T1/T2 contrast with TR/TE sliders (spinEcho). Its notes even mention k-space. So this candidate's T1/T2 sliders, 'echo time turns fat bright or dark' and the 1D-gradient-equals-Fourier step repeat that page. What is new: 2D phase and frequency encoding filling k-space line by line, a Bloch-equation spin echo (dephasing and refocusing), and the artefacts from editing k-space (centre only, edges only, skipped lines giving aliasing or ghosts). Narrow the page to those, with medical-imaging as a prerequisite to build on. The pitfall is also misleading: standard 2D MRI does acquire slice by slice (a slice-selective pulse with a gradient), so 'the gradient does not scan slice by slice' is wrong. Level 3 is honest (a BME MRI course), and the Shepp-Logan phantom needs no data.

title: Why clouds form, and why their bottoms are flat
interaction: Drag a bubble of air up from the warm ground: it swells and its thermometer drops about one degree for every hundred metres, until the invisible water it carries turns to droplets and the bubble turns white. Every bubble released from the same ground turns white at the same height, so the clouds have flat bottoms; make the day more humid and the cloud base drops, dry the air and clouds form higher or not at all. A last step blows the bubble over a mountain: it cools as it is pushed up the slope, rains on the side facing the wind, and comes down the far side drier and warmer than it started.
takeaway: Rising air swells and cools, and a cloud appears at exactly the height where the air gets cold enough for its water to turn into droplets, which is why the bottoms of clouds are flat.
needsSource: none (dry-adiabatic cooling of a parcel and the Magnus saturation formula, the standard textbook model)
pitfall: It is not colder up a mountain because it is farther from the Sun: a few kilometres make no difference to sunlight; the air up there is cold because air that rises expands and cools. Clouds are not made of vapour: they are tiny droplets, each heavier than air, that stay up because they fall more slowly than the rising air beneath them.
why: UCAR Center for Science Education, 'Clouds and How They Form' (https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/clouds/how-clouds-form); NGSS MS-ESS2-4 on the changes of state in the water cycle.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) shows global convection, pressure systems and fronts; this page follows one bubble of air and one cloud, with no Coriolis and no map.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Following one rising bubble of air explains flat cloud bottoms, cold mountains and the rain shadow with no formulas, an excellent level-0 mechanism distinct from atmosphere-weather's global view.

build 5: A rising parcel with the dry adiabatic lapse rate, the Magnus saturation formula and a moist lapse rate over the mountain (foehn) is the standard textbook model: tiny, exact and right for level 0.
verifyNote: It is distinct enough: dew-and-fog (pool L0) cools air by contact, and water-cycle and global-water-cycle cover the cycle and budgets, while this page's mechanism is cooling by rising and expansion, the flat base at the lifting condensation level and the rain shadow. A parcel model with the Magnus formula needs no data, and the level is honest for L0 (counts and comparisons only). The numbers are right: about 10 °C per km dry, and the cloud base drops as humidity rises (about 125 m for each degree between the temperature and the dew point). Two factual faults. (a) The interaction says the bubble's 1 °C per 100 m 'is also why it is colder on a mountain', but the air around a mountain cools by only about 6.5 °C per km on average, so the mountain should not show the parcel's dry rate. (b) The pitfall says clouds are 'not lighter than air', which is muddled: a growing cumulus is buoyant air, warmer and lighter than its surroundings, that happens to carry droplets. The droplets are what is heavier, and they stay up because they fall more slowly than the air rises. The droplets point also overlaps how-rain-forms, so it should be kept brief.

title: How a wildfire crosses a forest, or stops
interaction: A square forest of trees on a grid; light the left edge and watch the fire pass from each burning tree to its neighbours, leaving ash. One control: how densely the trees are planted. At half density the fire burns a few trees and dies, at two-thirds it nearly always crosses the forest, and around six in ten it is a coin toss, with a tally of how far the fire got over many runs; then cut a firebreak and find the width that stops it, or add wind so the fire jumps one extra tree downwind.
takeaway: In a big forest, a fire's chance of crossing does not grow gradually with how many trees there are: it flips from almost never to almost always over a narrow band of density, so removing a few trees or cutting a gap can stop a fire that would otherwise get through.
pitfall: The tipping density (about 59% for four neighbours on a square grid) belongs to the grid and the rule, not to forests; real fires also depend on wind, slope, moisture and fuel, which the page says it leaves out.
why: The NetLogo Fire model, one of the most used models in the NetLogo library, documents the sharp transition near 59% density: https://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/Fire
overlapWith: epidemics: spread through a moving crowd with a threshold set by immunity; this page is spread on a fixed grid where the threshold is set by how many cells there are (percolation). Pool neighbours life-on-a-grid and cellular-automata are rule-based grids with no randomness or threshold; fire-triangle is what a fire needs chemically.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A real percolation model a 10-year-old can run, with a surprising sharp threshold as the takeaway; distinct from epidemics (moving crowd) and the deterministic grid candidates.

build 5: Site percolation on a grid, repeated over many runs to tally crossings near the 0.59 threshold, plus firebreak and wind neighbourhoods, is a small, honest stochastic model that runs fast in the browser.
verifyNote: Distinct from epidemics (SIR in a moving crowd) and ecosystems: no catalogue page shows site percolation on a fixed grid. The physics checks out: the site-percolation threshold on the square lattice with four neighbours is about 0.5927, and the NetLogo Fire model shows it. The model is a trivial cellular automaton, needs no data, and the level-0 framing ("six in ten", tallies) holds up. One small correction: the jump is only sharp on a large grid, and the line "which is why thinning and firebreaks work" claims too much about real fire management, so the takeaway is tightened.

title: Where wind comes from: the sea breeze
interaction: A coast in cross-section, land on one side and sea on the other, filled with air drawn as drifting particles. Drag the Sun across the sky: by afternoon the land is warmer than the sea, the air over it rises, and air from the sea slides in underneath as a breeze that a flag on the beach shows. At night the land cools faster than the water and the breeze turns around and blows out to sea.
takeaway: Uneven heating is enough to make a wind: by day air slides in from over the cooler sea to replace the warm air rising over the land, and at night the land cools below the sea and the breeze turns around.
needsSource: none (a small 2D buoyant-convection solver on a coarse grid, with the sea slower to warm than the land)
pitfall: Warm air does not rise because heat goes up: it rises because it is lighter than the cooler air around it, which pushes it up. And not every wind is a sea breeze: big weather systems are steered by Earth's spin, which this page leaves out.
why: NOAA JetStream, 'The Sea Breeze' (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/ocean/sea-breeze); NGSS MS-ESS2-5 on air masses moving from high to low pressure.
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather (level 2) heats a whole spinning globe into convection cells and winds with Coriolis; this page heats one beach and gets one wind, no rotation.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The canonical first explanation of wind, from uneven heating, with a reversal at night; one control (the Sun), and distinct from the rotating globe in atmosphere-weather.

build 4: A coarse 2D Boussinesq convection solver (stable-fluids style) with land and sea of different heat capacity, forced by the Sun's angle, is buildable at interactive rates and gives the reversal honestly, though it is the heaviest solver in this batch.
verifyNote: It is distinct from atmosphere-weather (level 2: a globe, Coriolis, cells), and a coarse 2D Boussinesq convection solver runs easily in a browser. The level-0 framing is honest, and the pitfall about buoyancy is correct. But the takeaway claims too much: it says wind in general is air moving from cool to warm. Large-scale winds are steered by Earth's rotation and pressure systems and blow mostly along isobars, which is the very content of atmosphere-weather. The takeaway has to be narrowed to the local, thermally driven breeze. The cited standard is fine: the MS-ESS2-5 clarification mentions air flowing from high to low pressure, and MS-ESS2-6 is about unequal heating.

title: Tsunamis: a wave as long as the ocean is deep
interaction: A slice of the Pacific from Japan to California with the real sea floor under it. Jolt the floor up near the trench and watch the hump race across the deep ocean at airliner speed while a clock counts the hours and markers show arrival times; a speed gauge follows the depth, fast over the abyss and slowing over the shelf, where the wave bunches up and grows from under a metre to many metres. Drag the floor to change a shelf's slope or add an island, and compare with a wind wave of the same height, which barely notices the depth.
takeaway: A tsunami is a shallow-water wave even over the deepest ocean, so its speed is set by the depth alone: it crosses an ocean in hours, is barely visible at sea, and rears up only when it reaches the shallows.
needs: An ocean depth transect from NOAA's ETOPO 2022 relief model; the one-dimensional shallow-water equations run on that profile (a single transect ignores spreading across the ocean, so the far-shore height is an upper bound: state it on the page).
pitfall: A tsunami is not a towering surf wave: at the coast it arrives as a fast-rising flood lasting minutes, often after the sea draws back; and it is not a tidal wave, tides have nothing to do with it.
why: NOAA's tsunami facts (speed is the square root of gravity times depth, about 765 km/h over 4,600 m of water) answer the common 'how do tsunamis work': https://noaa.gov/node/10981
overlapWith: beach-waves (pool, level 0): wind waves slowing and breaking on a beach; this page is a wave longer than the ocean is deep, with its speed set by depth all the way across and real travel times. earthquakes: the seismic waves inside the Earth; this page is the water wave an undersea quake launches.
needsSource: ETOPO 2022 (NOAA NCEI, US government work, public domain).
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Speed set by depth (the shallow-water wave), with shoaling over real bathymetry, is a striking and honest level-1 mechanism with high public demand; distinct from earthquakes.

build 5: The 1D shallow-water equations on an ETOPO 2022 transect (public domain) are a textbook small PDE that runs at interactive rates, and the speed √(gh), the shoaling and the travel times are real outputs; the stated upper-bound caveat for one transect is honest.
verifyNote: No existing page covers tsunamis. earthquakes shows seismic waves inside the Earth. waves-interference shows superposition and standing waves, not depth-limited speed or shoaling. The pool's beach-waves (L0) is wind waves breaking. Level 1 is honest: speed = sqrt(g*depth) is high-school algebra, and the prerequisites (waves-interference L1, earthquakes L1) are not above it. A linear 1D shallow-water solver on a few thousand cells of an ETOPO transect runs at interactive rates, and the entry honestly flags the 1D upper bound. NCEI metadata says ETOPO 2022 is not subject to copyright and may be redistributed at no cost. The takeaway (about 765 km/h over 4,600 m, per NOAA) and the pitfall (flood-like arrival, frequent drawback, not tidal) are correct.

title: The carbonate-silicate thermostat
interaction: A box model in which volcanoes outgas CO2, silicate weathering removes it at a rate that rises with temperature and rainfall (the Walker, Hays and Kasting feedback), and a one-layer energy balance sets the temperature. Dim the young Sun to seventy percent and run a million years: CO2 piles up until weathering catches up and the planet stays unfrozen. Freeze the planet to stop weathering and watch CO2 climb for millions of years until the ice gives way; move the planet outward or switch off the volcanoes to find where the thermostat fails.
takeaway: Over millions of years rock weathering acts as a thermostat, because a warmer, wetter planet draws down CO2 faster, which is why Earth stayed habitable under a brightening Sun and how a Snowball Earth ends.
pitfall: This thermostat works over hundreds of thousands to millions of years and does nothing about fossil-fuel CO2 on human timescales; the fast carbon cycle and the slow one are different pages. It is the leading explanation of the faint young Sun paradox, not a settled one: the page should not present a single CO2 history as known.
why: MIT OCW 12.842 Climate Physics and Chemistry, Lecture 4 'The Faint Young Sun Paradox, the geochemical C cycle and climate on geologic time scales': https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/12-842-climate-physics-and-chemistry-fall-2008/resources/part1_lec4
overlapWith: carbon-cycle: that page runs the fast cycle over decades with human emissions; this page runs the slow rock cycle over millions of years and shows the feedback that makes it a thermostat.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A genuine level-3 Walker-Hays-Kasting box model coupled to energy balance, with faint-Sun and snowball experiments; distinct from the fast carbon cycle over decades.
build 5: The Walker-Hays-Kasting weathering feedback with a one-layer energy balance is a two-variable ODE box model that integrates over millions of years in milliseconds and needs no data.
verifyNote: It is distinct from carbon-cycle (L1: the fast cycle and human emissions over decades) and greenhouse-effect (L1: energy balance, no weathering feedback). The Walker-Hays-Kasting box model with a one-layer energy balance is a small ODE and easily client-side, needing no data beyond published parameters (such as the ~17.7 K e-folding temperature). Level 3 is honest: the topic is taught in graduate and upper-level climate courses (MIT 12.842, UChicago GEOS 32060), and the prerequisites are both L1. The takeaway and pitfall are sound. The page should still call the faint-young-Sun resolution the leading explanation, since higher early CO2 is debated alongside other factors. The weak point is the 'why' signal: it admits the course week was unconfirmed, so replace it with the MIT OCW 12.842 lecture, which covers this exact content.

title: Weather forecasts: why they come as odds
interaction: A ring of forty weather cells round a latitude circle (the Lorenz-96 model) runs as a strip of colour, the true weather on top and the reader's forecast started from a measurement of it with adjustable error. Launch one forecast and watch it track the truth for a few days and then diverge; launch fifty from slightly different starts and watch the fan open, narrow on some days and wide on others, with the spread plotted against the actual error. Shrink the measurement error tenfold and the useful range grows only a few days; make the model slightly wrong and the fan goes confident and wrong; then run the forecast-observe-correct cycle and watch the analysis stay close.
takeaway: Because small errors in today's weather keep doubling every few days, a single forecast loses its skill after a week or two; forecasters run many from slightly different starts, and where the runs agree the forecast is sure and where they fan out it is not.
pitfall: Chaos does not make forecasting useless: the useful range differs from day to day, and the ensemble shows which days are which. But an ensemble's spread is not automatically a trustworthy probability: a slightly wrong model gives a narrow, confident fan that misses, which is why forecasters check spread against error and calibrate. A '70% chance of rain' means a 70% chance at any one spot, not rain over 70% of the area or 70% of the day.
why: ECMWF's training course teaches ensemble prediction with the Lorenz-96 model, and 'why are weather forecasts wrong' is a perennial public question: https://events.ecmwf.int/event/405/contributions/4491/attachments/2523/4335/lorenz-part1.pdf
overlapWith: chaos-fractals: two double pendulums diverge; this page is what forecasters do about that: many starts, spread as a forecast of uncertainty, and the correction cycle. atmosphere-weather is the physics of circulation, with no forecasting.
needsSource: none (Lorenz 1996 equations)
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A real mechanism (Lorenz-96 ensembles, spread against error, and the assimilation cycle) that people meet every day in forecasts; it starts where chaos-fractals stops and is honestly university atmospheric science.

build 5: Lorenz-96 with 40 variables is cheap enough that fifty RK4 members plus a small ensemble Kalman filter run easily in the browser; the model is the standard testbed forecasters use and needs no data.
verifyNote: The page is distinct and buildable. chaos-fractals (L2) only shows divergence. A 40-variable Lorenz-96 with a 50-member ensemble and an ensemble Kalman filter runs easily in the browser, and data assimilation is university atmospheric-science material, with prerequisites at L2. But the takeaway overstates: a single forecast is not 'useless past a week or so'. Operational deterministic skill reaches about 10 days in midlatitudes, and the intrinsic limit is about two weeks. Synoptic error-doubling estimates range from about 1.5 to 5 days, so 'a couple of days' is acceptable. The pitfall also muddles the probability point: a raw ensemble fraction is exactly a count of members, and calibration is a separate post-processing step. The interaction already shows the real lesson, an over-confident wrong fan from a biased model. Rewrite the takeaway and pitfall.

title: Ocean acidification & carbonate chemistry
interaction: Slide atmospheric CO2 from the pre-industrial 280 ppm past 1,000 ppm while the page solves the seawater carbonate system (the dissociation constants of carbonic acid in seawater, with alkalinity held fixed): pH falls, dissolved CO2 and bicarbonate rise, carbonate ion falls, and the aragonite saturation state drops below one first in cold water. A Bjerrum plot shows the species shifting with pH, a temperature slider shows why polar seas get there first, and the Revelle factor shows why the ocean's uptake slows as it fills.
takeaway: Adding CO2 to seawater does not just lower its pH, it consumes carbonate ions, the building block of shells, and cold water runs short of them first.
needs: Published empirical fits for seawater equilibrium constants as functions of temperature and salinity, the same ones CO2SYS uses: K0 (Weiss 1974), K1 and K2 of carbonic acid (Lueker et al. 2000), borate KB (Dickson 1990) and total boron (Uppström 1974) for the alkalinity, and aragonite and calcite solubility (Mucci 1983). These are published coefficients, retyped and cited. Cross-check the solver against PyCO2SYS (open source, GPL-3) in a model test.
pitfall: The ocean is not becoming acid (its pH stays above 7); acidification means moving toward acid, and the harm is the loss of carbonate ion, not corrosive water.
why: University of Texas MNS 193 Ocean and Estuarine Acidification, a course built around CO2SYS carbonate-chemistry calculations: https://hulab.utmsi.utexas.edu/OA_class/index.htm
overlapWith: acids-bases: that page titrates a single acid and counts hydrogen ions; this page solves the coupled carbonate equilibria of seawater and reads off the carbonate ion and saturation state that acids-bases never reaches.
needsSource: none beyond published equilibrium-constant fits (Weiss 1974; Lueker et al. 2000; Dickson 1990; Mucci 1983), verified against PyCO2SYS (GPL-3, used only as a test oracle, not shipped)
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Seawater carbonate equilibria with saturation state and the Revelle factor are a real coupled model that acids-bases never reaches; the subject is in high demand and the level is honest.

build 5: Solving the seawater carbonate system with fixed alkalinity is a one-variable root find using published empirical constants (Lueker/Millero/Mucci fits, facts from the literature), which is the honest CO2SYS model and runs instantly.
verifyNote: It is distinct from acids-bases (L1 titration and the pH scale) and carbon-cycle (L1 reservoirs and flows). Neither solves the seawater carbonate system or reaches carbonate ion, saturation state or the Revelle factor. Level 3 is honest: it is chemical oceanography with CO2SYS, and the prerequisites (L1 and L2) are not above it. Fixed-alkalinity speciation is a 1D root-find, so the page is instant client-side. The takeaway is correct: polar and cold waters reach aragonite undersaturation first, through higher CO2 solubility and lower alkalinity, and seasonal undersaturation is already observed in some polar seas. The pitfall is correct. Improvement: name the specific published constants, because the needs field is vague. Borate must be included in the alkalinity, or pH comes out wrong.

title: Radiative transfer & the climate column
interaction: A column of air from the surface to the stratosphere, solved with the two-stream radiative transfer equations for a grey gas plus an infrared window, with convection adjusting any layer steeper than the chosen lapse rate. Slide the infrared optical depth (the CO2 amount) and the lapse rate and watch the temperature profile, the tropopause and the emission height move, while a side panel shows which layer the escaping infrared leaves from. Close the window to make the gas fully grey and watch the stratosphere stop cooling as CO2 rises; switch convection off to see pure radiative equilibrium and its unstable lower layers.
takeaway: Adding greenhouse gas raises the height from which the planet radiates to space, and because air is colder higher up the whole column below must warm to restore the balance, while the stratosphere above it cools.
pitfall: Greenhouse gases do not trap heat like a lid or reflect infrared; the column warms because the effective emission level rises into colder air. A band that is saturated at the surface still warms the planet, because emission from higher, thinner layers is what matters. Stratospheric cooling is not automatic for any absorber: in a perfectly grey atmosphere the stratosphere's temperature does not change, and it cools here because part of the infrared escapes through the window.
why: Pierrehumbert's Principles of Planetary Climate courseware, chapter 4 grey radiative-convective equilibrium notebook: https://users.physics.ox.ac.uk/~pierrehumbert/PrinciplesPlanetaryClimate/Courseware/PlanetaryClimateCourseware2/ChapterScripts/Chapter4/Chapter4.html
overlapWith: greenhouse-effect: that page balances sunlight in against infrared out with adjustable CO2 in a zero-dimensional budget; this page adds the vertical structure, which is where the emission height, the lapse rate and stratospheric cooling live.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The emission-height and lapse-rate column is the textbook university step beyond greenhouse-effect's zero-dimensional balance, and it explains stratospheric cooling with the real two-stream model.
build 5: A grey two-stream column with a window band and convective adjustment (Manabe-Wetherald style) is a classic tiny model that relaxes in milliseconds and needs no data.
verifyNote: Distinct: the existing greenhouse-effect page (src/routes/greenhouse-effect/climate.ts) is a single leaky-greenhouse layer plus a two-layer ocean energy budget. It has no vertical temperature profile, lapse rate, convective adjustment or emission height. A semi-grey two-stream column with convective adjustment is a standard level-3 model (Pierrehumbert ch. 4) and solves in milliseconds in the browser, with no external data. The takeaway is physically right, with one catch. In a purely grey gas the stratosphere settles at the skin temperature, which does not depend on optical depth, so a grey column will not show stratospheric cooling. Cooling appears only through the infrared window (Goessling and Bathiany's window-grey model, https://esd.copernicus.org/preprints/esd-2016-8/esd-2016-8-manuscript-version4.pdf). Recent work (Cohen, Pincus and Polvani 2026) stresses that it depends on the gas's spectroscopy. The interaction and pitfall should say so, so the page doesn't imply that every greenhouse gas cools the stratosphere.

title: Comets and their tails
interaction: Scrub a comet along its real stretched orbit, far out and frozen, then swinging in close to the Sun. As it warms, gas and dust stream off it, and the tail always points away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is going, so on the way out the comet flies tail-first. Two tails appear: a straight blue gas tail pushed by the solar wind and a curved dust tail of grains that lag along the orbit; zoom in to see the grains leave.
takeaway: A comet's tails are pushed out by the Sun, not left behind by its motion, so the gas tail always points straight away from the Sun and the comet leaves tail-first, while the dust tail bends back along the path it has travelled.
needs: Orbital elements of comet 1P/Halley (perihelion distance, eccentricity, period) from the JPL Small-Body Database: a few published numbers, typed into the model and free to reuse with the credit 'Courtesy NASA/JPL-Caltech' under JPL's open data policy.
needsSource: JPL Small-Body Database, Halley's orbital elements (NASA/JPL measured facts, free to reuse with credit)
pitfall: The tail does not trail behind like exhaust, and a comet is not a burning rock: it is ice and dust turning to gas in sunlight.
why: NASA Space Place, 'What Is a Comet?' (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/comets/en/); England KS2 Year 5, the movement of bodies relative to the Sun.
overlapWith: orbits-kepler (level 1) launches bodies into ellipses; this page uses one real ellipse and asks only which way the tail points.
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A clear, surprising mechanism (the Sun blows the tail away, so the comet leaves tail-first) that a 10-year-old can scrub, and it is distinct from orbits-kepler.

title: Earth is a ball
interaction: Drag a ship out to sea and watch it from the shore. On a flat world it only shrinks, and binoculars bring all of it back. On the round world its hull sinks out of sight before its sails as the sea bulges up between you and it (the curve drawn exaggerated, the distances real). Binoculars cannot bring the hull back, but climbing a cliff can. Then walk a little figure around the globe: wherever it stands its feet point to the middle, and a dropped ball falls toward the middle too, so nobody on the far side falls off.
takeaway: The world is a ball, so the sea itself hides the bottom of a distant ship, and 'down' means toward the middle wherever you stand.
needsSource: none (the geometry of a sphere: horizon distance from eye height and the height hidden beyond it; gravity drawn toward the centre)
pitfall: People on the far side are not upside down and do not have to hold on: the page draws no fixed up arrow anywhere. The ship does not vanish because it got too small, and magnifying it does not bring the hull back. The bulge is drawn much bigger than it really is, and air bends light a little so you see slightly farther than the plain geometry says; the page does not claim exact distances.
why: NGSS 5-PS2-1: 'Support an argument that the gravitational force exerted by Earth on objects is directed down', with 'down' pointing toward the center of the spherical Earth (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/5-ps2-1-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions); England KS2 Year 5: 'describe the sun, Earth and moon as approximately spherical bodies'.
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon (level 1) tilts and orbits the Earth; this page never moves it, only shows that it is round and which way down is.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: An ideal level-0 page: a familiar experience (the ship hull disappearing first), one drag control, and the 'down means toward the middle' idea that prepares for newtons-laws and sun-earth-moon.

build 4: Horizon distance and hidden height from eye height are an exact geometric construction and the falling ball is trivial radial gravity; it is a small honest model at level 0 and needs no data.
verifyNote: Not a duplicate: sun-earth-moon moves a tilted Earth and never shows that it is round or which way is down. The level is honest (NGSS 5-PS2-1 and KS2 Y5 both ask for exactly this), and the model is real sphere geometry: the horizon distance and the height hidden behind it, computed from eye height. Two small improvements keep it honest. Light bending in the air (refraction) lets you see somewhat farther than straight-line geometry predicts (roughly 15% in typical conditions), so the page should not claim exact hull-hiding distances. Also, at true scale the bulge is far too small to see, so the drawing must say the curve is exaggerated. The pitfall 'it doesn't vanish because it got too small' is best shown by a binoculars toggle: zooming in brings back a small ship but not a hidden hull. That makes the takeaway observable without any text.

title: Leap years: why February gets an extra day
interaction: A calendar wheel turns inside Earth's orbit: one lap of the Sun takes 365 days and about a quarter more, so each New Year falls a quarter-day short. Scrub forward with no leap days and watch the first day of summer slide through the calendar, a month after a century and into winter after seven or eight centuries; switch on 'one extra day every four years' and the slide almost stops; zoom out over a thousand years to see the small drift that is left and the 'skip every hundred, keep every four hundred' rule that fixes it.
takeaway: A year is not a whole number of days, so a calendar without leap days drifts out of step with the seasons; an extra day every four years, with a few skipped, keeps them matched.
pitfall: A leap day fixes the calendar, not the orbit; nothing about the seasons changes. The rule is not simply every four years: 1900 was not a leap year and 2000 was.
why: NASA/JPL Education, 'Doing the math on why we have leap day' (interest spikes every leap year): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/doing-the-math-on-why-we-have-leap-day/
overlapWith: sun-earth-moon: why there are seasons; this page is why the calendar needs correcting to stay lined up with them.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Calendar drift is a genuine mechanism, explained with counts of days, that people ask about, and it is distinct from sun-earth-moon's seasons.

build 5: Calendar drift is exact arithmetic of the tropical year (about 365.2422 days, a published constant) against the Julian and Gregorian rules, a clear algorithm whose drift is visible on the wheel.
verifyNote: Distinct from sun-earth-moon, which explains why there are seasons, not how a calendar stays lined up with them. It suits L0: it starts from an everyday object (February 29), the numbers are only counts and comparisons (a quarter of a day), and one toggle drives each step. The model is the real arithmetic of the tropical year (about 365.2422 days) against the calendar rules. The numbers check out. Without leap days the calendar slips about 0.24 days a year: roughly a month in about 125 years, and the summer solstice reaches winter after about 750 years ('seven or eight centuries'). The Julian every-four-years rule leaves about one day per 128 years, roughly 8 days in a thousand years, the 'small drift' the 1582 Gregorian reform fixed. The pitfall about 1900 and 2000 is correct. No external data is needed; the length of the year is a standard astronomical constant.

title: Interferometry & aperture synthesis
interaction: Place radio dishes on a map and pick a model sky; every pair of dishes samples the sky's Fourier transform at one point and its mirror image, and as the Earth turns each pair traces a pair of arcs in the uv plane. Watch the dirty beam and the dirty image form from whatever the array has sampled: two dishes see only stripes, a dozen over six hours see the source. Run CLEAN step by step, subtracting the beam from the brightest point until the image emerges, and compare it with the truth; shrink the array to lose resolution, spread it to lose the extended emission.
takeaway: An array of small telescopes can see as sharply as one dish as wide as the array, because what it measures is the sky's Fourier transform, and the Earth's rotation fills in the gaps.
needs: No external data required: model skies (point sources, a disc, a jet) are generated in code and the model is a 2D FFT plus Hogbom CLEAN. Optional real array layouts (VLA Y with 120-degree arms; ALMA configurations from the CASA simulator's antenna-configuration files, CASA being open source under the GPL), or the coordinates published in open-access papers.
pitfall: An interferometer does not gain the collecting area of a filled dish, only its resolution, and the dirty image is not a photograph of the sky but of what was sampled.
why: NRAO Synthesis Imaging Workshop, the graduate course on aperture synthesis theory and technique: https://aas.org/events/2022-02/18th-synthesis-imaging-workshop
overlapWith: light-optics: that page forms images with lenses and never treats resolution as a Fourier limit; medical-imaging also computes an image from indirect measurements, but from projections combined by filtered back-projection, whereas this page fills the Fourier plane with correlations between pairs of separated telescopes and deconvolves with CLEAN.
needsSource: none required; optional array layouts from CASA's open-source configuration files (GPL) or open-access papers
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A genuine level-3 mechanism (uv coverage, dirty beam, CLEAN) built on fourier-transform, and distinct from the single-dish telescopes candidate.
build 5: Baselines tracing uv arcs, a gridded 2D FFT for the dirty beam and image, and Högbom CLEAN on a 128-256 pixel grid are small, exact and fast in the browser, with no data needed.
verifyNote: Distinct: no Space page covers telescopes or interferometry; gravitational-waves has a laser interferometer measuring length change, not imaging; medical-imaging is the nearest mechanism (an image computed from indirect samples) but uses projections and back-projection in CT, not Fourier samples from correlated pairs. Level 3 is honest: aperture synthesis is graduate or master's material (NRAO Synthesis Imaging Workshop; Chalmers RRY131; Manchester PHYS40491), and the prerequisites sit at levels 1-2. It can be built in the browser: a 2D FFT on a 128-256 grid, uv tracks from Earth-rotation geometry, and Hogbom CLEAN all run at interactive rates (APSYNSIM, a GPL Python teaching tool, does exactly this on the desktop). The takeaway and pitfall are correct, and so is 'spread it to lose the extended emission': the shortest baseline sets the largest recoverable scale. Small fixes: each baseline samples a Hermitian pair of uv points, not one; name the optional open data (array layouts) in needs; record the medical-imaging contrast in overlapWith.

title: The three-body problem & Lagrange points
interaction: The circular restricted three-body problem, drawn in the frame that rotates with the two large bodies. Set the mass ratio (Sun-Jupiter, Sun-Earth, Earth-Moon, or a slider) and the five Lagrange points appear. Set the probe's energy (the Jacobi constant) and the forbidden regions shade in, opening gates at L1 and L2 as the energy rises. Drop a probe at L1 or L2 and it drifts away within months. Drop one near L4 and it wanders in a tadpole around the point for as long as the reader waits, as Jupiter's Trojans do. Push the mass ratio past about 1 in 26 and the same probe escapes. Nudge a starting position by a hair to run two probes side by side and watch their paths split.
takeaway: Three bodies have no general closed-form solution and nearby paths split apart, but there are five points where a small body can keep pace with the other two: three balanced on a knife edge, and two that are stable while the smaller mass is light enough.
pitfall: L1 and L2 are not places where gravity cancels. A spacecraft there circles the Sun in exactly one Earth year because the combined pull (Earth's pull partly offsets the Sun's at L1 and adds to it at L2) is exactly what that orbit needs, and it still needs station-keeping. The general three-body problem is not 'unsolvable': Sundman found a convergent series, but no closed formula and no long-term predictability.
why: MIT OCW 16.346 Astrodynamics, lecture 25 on the restricted problem of three bodies (Jacobi integral, surfaces of zero relative velocity): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/16-346-astrodynamics-fall-2008/resources/lec_25
overlapWith: orbits-kepler: that page adds a second planet to see two bodies disturb each other; this page moves to the rotating frame, where the forbidden regions and the stability of the five points become visible.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The rotating-frame CR3BP with Jacobi zero-velocity curves, tadpole orbits and chaotic divergence is a superb level-3 manipulate page that orbits-kepler does not reach.
build 5: The circular restricted three-body problem in the rotating frame, with Jacobi zero-velocity curves and RK integration of probes, is exact, small and fast.
verifyNote: Distinct and honest. orbits-kepler adds a second planet in the inertial frame, while this page uses the rotating frame, the Jacobi constant, zero-velocity curves and the stability of the Lagrange points, which is standard university astrodynamics (MIT OCW 16.346). The circular restricted three-body problem integrates easily in the browser. The takeaway and pitfall need correcting. 'There is no formula for the motion' is too strong: Sundman (1912) found a convergent series solution. The accurate claim is that there is no general closed-form solution and that nearby starts diverge, which is also what the side-by-side probes actually show. The pitfall says the two pulls 'add' at L1 and L2, but at L1 Earth's pull partly cancels the Sun's; only at L2 do they add. The stability of L4 and L5 also depends on the mass ratio: they are stable only below Routh's limit, mu < 0.0385, which Sun-Jupiter, Sun-Earth and Earth-Moon all satisfy. A mass-ratio slider that crosses this limit makes the claim 'two stable points' visible rather than asserted.

title: Life on a grid
interaction: Paint a few squares on a grid and press step: every square counts its live neighbours at once, and the three rules (lonely dies, crowded dies, exactly three neighbours gives birth) show as the counts on each square. Press play and find the shapes that blink, the ones that sit still and the glider that walks across the board. Change one number in a rule and watch the same seed grow, freeze or die.
takeaway: A rule about counting neighbours, applied to every square at once, makes things that blink, walk and grow that nobody drew.
pitfall: All squares update together from the previous picture, not one after another; a page that updates in place gets wrong patterns. And do not call Life 'random': the same seed gives the same future every time.

title: Secret codes & code-breaking
interaction: Turn the inner ring of a code wheel and type a message: each letter steps along the alphabet by the same amount, and your friend turns the ring back to read it. A spy who does not know the turn tries all 25 turns at once and the one that reads as words jumps out. Scramble the alphabet instead; now the spy counts the letters in the secret message and lines its bars up with the bars of ordinary English: the tallest few give E, T and A, half-words like TH_ appear, and the reader swaps the remaining letters until the message reads.
takeaway: A code that shifts every letter the same way falls to trying all 25 shifts, and a code that scrambles the alphabet falls to counting letters, because in a long message E stays the most common letter however it is disguised.
needs: English letter frequencies counted at build time by a script from a public-domain text, e.g. Project Gutenberg's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (public domain), not typed in from memory.
pitfall: A short message has too few letters for counting to work: show the counting fail on a one-line note and succeed on a paragraph, rather than pretending frequency analysis always works.
why: The National Cipher Challenge, the University of Southampton's codebreaking competition for school teams, starts every year with ciphers of this kind. https://www.cipherchallenge.org/
overlapWith: cryptography (level 2) covers key exchange, hashing and signatures with modular arithmetic; this page is pen-and-paper ciphers and the two ways they break, with no keys shared over a channel.
needsSource: A Project Gutenberg public-domain English text for the letter counts.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Caesar brute force and frequency analysis are real mechanisms done by counting, a classic primary and middle-school favourite, and clearly distinct from the level-2 cryptography page's key exchange and hashing.
build 5: Caesar brute force and substitution frequency analysis are exact algorithms, and letter counts from a public-domain Project Gutenberg text are freely computable at build time.
verifyNote: Distinct from cryptography (L2: key exchange, hashing and signatures), honestly level 0 (letter counts shown as bars), buildable, and its data source is fine (a Project Gutenberg text, public domain). But it overstates frequency analysis: lining up the bars by height finds E, T and A, and nothing more. Past the first few letters the ranks in English are close and change from text to text, so the reader has to fix the rest by spotting part-words. The interaction and takeaway are corrected to say so. leadsTo primes-modular-arithmetic (level 1) is valid.

title: Twenty questions: halving the haystack
interaction: Think of a number from 1 to 100 and answer the page's 'higher or lower' questions: a bar of candidates shrinks by half each answer and the counter stops at seven. Now find a word in a thousand-page dictionary by opening it in the middle, then in the middle of the right half, counting the opens, against a search that flips through every page. Then play animal twenty questions: each yes/no question hides half of the hundred animals on the board until one is left.
takeaway: A question that splits what is left in half finds the answer in a handful of steps, where checking one at a time takes hundreds.
needs: The animal board: the UCI Zoo dataset (101 animals, 16 yes/no and count features), CC BY 4.0.
pitfall: Halving needs either a list in order (the dictionary trick fails on a shuffled pile of pages) or a question that really splits what is left: show 'is it a penguin?' barely shrinking the board, and do not claim every yes/no question halves the pile.
why: England KS3 computing: 'several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking [for example, ones for sorting and searching]'; CS Unplugged Searching Algorithms ('How many guesses?', 'Divide and conquer', ages 5 to 10). https://www.csunplugged.org/en/topics/searching-algorithms/
overlapWith: sorting (level 1) shows how the cost of sorting grows with input size; nothing in the catalogue shows searching. This page shows halving against one-by-one on counts alone, without growth curves.
needsSource: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Zoo dataset (Forsyth 1990, DOI 10.24432/C5R59V), CC BY 4.0.
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Halving against one-by-one search is a core idea shown with counts only, from a game every child knows, and the catalogue has no searching page at all.

build 4: Binary search and a greedy question tree over the UCI Zoo dataset (101 animals, CC BY 4.0 under UCI's repository licence) are exact and tiny; real features will not split exactly in half, which the page must show honestly rather than claim perfect halving.
verifyNote: No existing page shows searching by halving. graph-search expands a frontier across a map, and compression (L2) measures bits of surprise with formulas. The counts are right: a number from 1 to 100 takes at most 7 guesses (2^7 = 128), and a 1000-page dictionary about 10 opens. Level 0 is honest (counts only, one question at a time). The UCI Zoo dataset (101 animals, yes/no features) is distributed by UCI under a Creative Commons licence, CC BY 4.0 like UCI's other datasets; the search snippet confirmed Creative Commons but cut off before the version, so the page should cite it with its DOI 10.24432/C5R59V. One small fix: the pitfall says halving needs a sorted list, but animal questions need no sorting, only questions that split the pile, so the pitfall now keeps the two cases apart.

title: How a computer plays a game: the search tree
interaction: Play noughts and crosses against the page and open its mind: a tree of the moves it is weighing, the leaves scored win, draw or loss and the scores passed up, the computer taking the best of its moves and assuming you take the worst for it. Switch to Connect Four, where the whole tree is too big, and set how many moves ahead it looks: at two it blunders, at six it is hard to beat, and with pruning off the count of positions examined rises about sevenfold per extra move; turn on pruning and watch whole branches greyed out, the count falling steeply with the chosen move unchanged. Build the scoring rule yourself from a palette of features (centre column, three in a row) and test it.
takeaway: A game-playing program looks ahead down a tree of moves, assumes the opponent plays its best, and picks the line with the best guaranteed outcome; how deep it can afford to look is set by how fast the tree grows.
pitfall: The program does not plan like a person; it counts. And it does not look at every possible game: depth is limited and the leaves are scored by a rule of thumb, which is why a better scoring rule can beat a deeper search.
why: 'How does a chess computer work' tutorials (freeCodeCamp's step-by-step chess AI) are among the most-read introductions to minimax: https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/simple-chess-ai-step-by-step-1d55a9266977
overlapWith: graph-search: searching a map for a route; this page searches a tree of moves against an opponent, where a value flows up instead of a path being found. monte-carlo-tree-search (pool, level 3) uses random playouts and AlphaGo; this page is the full deterministic search at level 1.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Minimax with depth and pruning is a vivid mechanism with a strong visitor draw, honest at level 1 with noughts and crosses and Connect Four, and distinct from graph-search because a value flows up the tree against an opponent.

build 5: Full minimax for noughts and crosses and depth-limited alpha-beta for Connect Four (about 7^6 ≈ 120k nodes at depth 6, fine in a Web Worker) are exact and interactive, with real node counts; no data.
verifyNote: Distinct from graph-search (a path through a map, with no opponent and no value passed back up the tree), from reinforcement-learning (values learned in a grid world) and from the pool's monte-carlo-tree-search (random playouts and AlphaGo, level 3). Minimax with alpha-beta pruning runs at interactive rates in a browser: the full noughts-and-crosses tree is tiny, and Connect Four at depth 6 is about 7^6, or 120 thousand positions, fewer with pruning. Level 1 is a slight stretch, since alpha-beta usually comes in a first university AI course, but minimax on noughts and crosses is common in high-school computing and the page needs no formulas. One small fix: the 'about sevenfold' figure holds only with pruning off, so the interaction now says that.

title: Caches & the memory hierarchy
interaction: Choose a program's access pattern (sum an array row by row or column by column, walk a linked list, multiply matrices with and without blocking) and run it through a cache with adjustable size, line length, associativity and replacement policy; each access lights a line as a hit or a miss, and the miss count and the average memory access time plot live. Add a second level of cache and watch where the knee of the curve moves.
takeaway: The same program, doing the same arithmetic, takes many times more cycles waiting for memory or many times fewer, depending only on whether it touches memory in an order the cache can exploit.
pitfall: A bigger cache is not always better: a direct-mapped cache thrashes on a stride equal to its size however large it is, and the unit moved is a whole line, never a byte, so a miss costs the same for one byte as for sixty-four.
why: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, Unit 14 'Multilevel memories: locality, performance, caches' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/calendar
overlapWith: cpu: that page single-steps instructions against a flat memory that answers instantly; this page makes memory itself the model and shows why one access costs one cycle and the next two hundred.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A cache simulator with real parameters, where row against column order changes the miss rate, is a core systems mechanism at the right level, with a strong visual and no overlap with cpu's flat memory.
build 5: A set-associative cache simulator fed by real address traces of row/column sums, a linked-list walk and blocked matrix multiply is exact, fast and produces the hit/miss curves itself.
verifyNote: Distinct from cpu (L2), whose memory answers instantly, and from gpu. It is genuinely level 3, covered in MIT 6.004 and in standard computer-architecture courses (Hennessy and Patterson). Buildable as a cache simulator running over address traces generated in the browser; it needs no external data. The facts are right: row-by-row and column-by-column summing differ sharply in miss rate, blocking cuts misses in matrix multiply, a direct-mapped cache thrashes when it alternates between two addresses a cache-size apart, and data moves in whole lines. One small fix: a single miss does cost about the same for one byte as for a whole line, but the takeaway's 'many times faster' should be shown as average memory access time in cycles, not wall-clock speed, so it is observable and honest.

title: Hash tables & Bloom filters
interaction: Insert keys into a table with chaining or open addressing and raise the load factor; every probe is drawn, and the measured mean probe length is plotted against the expected curve until the table resizes and rehashes. Then feed the same keys to a Bloom filter with an adjustable bit array and number of hash functions, query keys that were never inserted and watch the measured false-positive rate track the standard approximation (closely for large arrays, drifting above it for tiny ones); degrade the hash function with a slider and see both structures cluster.
takeaway: A good hash spreads keys evenly, so lookups stay constant-time until the table fills, and a Bloom filter trades a known, tunable false-positive rate for a fraction of the memory.
pitfall: A hash table's constant time is an average under a good hash, not a guarantee; the cryptographic hash of the cryptography page is a different tool; and a Bloom filter can only ever say 'definitely absent', never 'definitely present'.
why: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lecture 4 'Hashing' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes (Bloom filters appear in CMU 15-445's index lectures)
overlapWith: cryptography: that page shows a hash as a one-way fingerprint; here the hash is a fast bucket index, and the model is the statistics of collisions as the table fills.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Probe lengths and Bloom false-positive rates, measured against the real formulas, are core data-structure models that suit the site's 'real model' rule, and the page is distinct from cryptography's use of hashes.
build 5: Chaining and open addressing with measured probe lengths, resizing, and a Bloom filter whose measured false-positive rate tracks (1-e^{-kn/m})^k are exact and instant; no data.
verifyNote: No existing page covers hashing as an index: cryptography (L2) shows the avalanche of a one-way hash, and sorting covers comparisons, not collisions. The level is honest, since hashing is taught in MIT 6.006 (a second-year CS course), and the prerequisites sorting and binary are both L1. The model is pure algorithm, so it is easily client-side and needs no data. The takeaway and pitfall are correct: a Bloom filter has no false negatives. The page should say the measured rate tracks it closely for large filters, which a small-bit-array slider can show.

title: Barcodes at the checkout
interaction: Drag a scanner's red line across a barcode (a UPC-A, the 12-digit form found on many products) and watch what it sees, a trace of dark and light over time, then step through it: a start mark, six groups of stripes, a middle mark, six more and an end mark, each group of two bars and two gaps one digit. Scan slowly, fast or at a slant and the widths all stretch together, so the digits come out the same; scan it upside down and the scanner tells, from the left groups looking different from the right ones, which way to read. Smudge one stripe and the last digit, a check digit, turns the light red: the number is wrong, scan again.
takeaway: A barcode is a number written as stripe widths, read as proportions so that speed and angle do not matter, with a last digit that catches a misread; the price is looked up afterwards.
needsSource: none; the UPC-A/EAN-13 symbol layout (95 modules, 7 per digit, L/G/R patterns, check digit) is public structural information (GS1 General Specifications; Wikipedia 'International Article Number', CC BY-SA, for the parity table).
pitfall: The barcode does not contain the price or the product name; it is a number the till looks up. The scanner reads ratios of widths, not absolute sizes, which is why the code can be printed at any size.
why: 'Barcode' averaged about 29,200 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Barcode/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).

judgeNotes: build 5: A real EAN-13 encoder, decoder and check digit plus a scan-line trace whose widths scale with speed and angle is a small, exact model; the layout is in the public GS1 specification.
fit-level 4: A familiar object with a real mechanism (widths read as ratios, plus a check digit) that a 10-year-old can explore without formulas, distinct from binary and from the QR candidate.
verifyNote: No existing page covers barcodes. binary is about bits, and this page is about width patterns, reading by proportion and a check digit. Level 0 is honest if the check digit is shown as a pass/fail light and not as a weighted sum. The model (EAN/UPC module patterns, decoding by ratios, the check digit) is a small algorithm. The layout is a published fact, also documented on Wikipedia, so no data licence is needed. The pitfall is correct. There is one factual flaw in the interaction: an EAN-13 has 13 digits, but only 12 groups of stripes appear. The first digit is hidden in the odd/even pattern of the left six groups. Either use UPC-A (12 digits, 6 + 6, all visible), which is the same symbol as EAN-13 with a leading 0, or say where the 13th digit lives. Reading upside down works because the left and right halves use different patterns, and the page should show that.

title: QR codes
interaction: Type a short message and watch it become a square of black and white cells, built the real way: the three big corner squares that tell a camera where the code is and which way up, then the message as cells, then spare cells computed from the message. Point a drawn camera at it from any angle and it reads. Now paint over cells with a brush: the message still comes out, and a counter shows how many cells are damaged; keep painting and find the moment it fails, then paint over a corner square instead, which fails at once.
takeaway: A QR code carries its message plus spare cells computed from it, so a scratched or half-covered code still reads, until too much of the message is spoiled or a corner finder is hidden.
needs: None to ship; the page runs a real encoder and decoder (open-source implementations of the QR standard exist under MIT and Apache 2.0, e.g. qrcode-generator and jsQR).
needsSource: none; an in-browser QR encoder and decoder (Reed-Solomon) under MIT/Apache 2.0.
pitfall: The three corner squares hold no message; they are for finding and orienting. The code is not read in a spiral or line by line, and the spare cells are not a copy of the message, so do not say the data is duplicated. The survivable damage (about 7 to 30 percent depending on the level chosen) is counted in damaged bytes, not cells or area: a scatter of specks can break a code that a single blot of the same size does not, so the cell counter is a guide, not a fixed limit.
why: NGSS 4-PS4-3: 'using a grid of 1's and 0's representing black and white to send information about a picture' (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/4-ps4-3-waves-and-their-applications-technologies-information-transfer); 'QR code' averaged about 388,000 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025.
overlapWith: error-correction (level 2): that page shows a Hamming code's parity checks on bits; this one is the object, with damage painted on and a count of cells survivable, and no arithmetic shown. barcode-stripes in this batch is the one-dimensional cousin with only a check digit.
judgeNotes: build 5: A real QR encoder with Reed-Solomon (MIT and Apache libraries exist) and a decoder run on painted damage give an exact failure point; for robustness the decoder should read the cell grid rather than a simulated camera image.

verifyNote: Distinct from error-correction, which is level 2 and shows Hamming parity checks on bits. This page is the physical object, its finder patterns, and Reed-Solomon tolerance to painted damage, with no arithmetic shown. An honest level 0. It is buildable: qrcode-generator (MIT) encodes, and jsQR (Apache-2.0) decodes a canvas rendered from the SVG. Covering a finder pattern does make decoding fail, as described. The pitfall misses one point: the recoverable fraction (7/15/25/30% for L/M/Q/H) is counted in damaged codewords (bytes), not cells. A count of cells cannot give a fixed failure threshold, because scattered damage touches more codewords than a compact blot. The format information next to the finders is also critical. The pitfall should say this, so the counter is not read as a universal cell budget.

title: Wi-Fi around the house
interaction: Place a router on a floor plan and the rooms fill with a signal map; drag the laptop around and its speed gauge follows the colour. Add walls, a brick one, a fridge, a fish tank, and watch each cut a shadow in the map and the gauge drop, as the link slows down to be heard through the loss. Switch the router to the faster, shorter-reach band and compare; then add a neighbour's router on the same channel and watch the two take turns.
takeaway: Wi-Fi is radio: walls and water eat it, the link slows down rather than breaking as the signal fades, and two networks on one channel must take turns.
needs: Attenuation per wall material at 2.4 and 5 GHz: NIST IR 6055, 'Electromagnetic Signal Attenuation in Construction Materials' (W. C. Stone, NIST, 1997; brick, concrete, drywall, glass, plywood, wet wood), for a multi-wall path-loss model; water (fish tank, people) from the same report's wet-material results or textbook absorption values.
needsSource: NIST IR 6055 (US federal government work, public domain; https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/IR/nistir6055.pdf).
pitfall: Wi-Fi is not the internet; a full signal to the router says nothing about the line out of the house. The signal does not stop at an edge: it fades gradually, and the devices then choose a slower, sturdier way of sending so that it can still be read, which is why the gauge drops step by step instead of cutting out. Walls are not perfect shadows either; reflections leak signal around them, which this simple wall-counting model leaves out.

overlapWith: wireless-signals (level 2): that page packs bits onto a carrier against noise; this one is where to put the router, computed from a wall-by-wall loss model, with speed shown as a gauge and no waveform.

A public-domain source exists: NIST IR 6055, Electromagnetic Signal Attenuation in Construction Materials (Stone, 1997, a US government work), which measured brick, concrete, drywall, glass, plywood and wet wood at 0.5 to 8 GHz. The intended point is that the slowdown is the devices choosing a sturdier, slower way to send, not the signal 'running out'. The page should also not imply that a wall's straight-line shadow is the whole story, since reflections fill in behind walls; a multi-wall model is a simplification and should be named as one.

title: How Shazam recognises a song
interaction: Play one of a few short clips synthesized in the page and watch its spectrogram scroll by; the page keeps only the brightest peaks, a constellation of dots, and turns pairs of nearby peaks into fingerprints (two pitches and the gap between them), building a tiny database of a dozen clips the same way. Record a few seconds of one clip with noise, a cough and a different start time added, and watch its fingerprints looked up: hits on the wrong clips scatter, hits on the right one line up at a single time offset, and the spike in the histogram names the song. Slide the noise up until the spike disappears.
takeaway: A song is recognised not by comparing sound but by matching a sparse set of peak pairs whose time gaps line up, which is why a few noisy seconds from the middle of a track are enough.
pitfall: It does not match the melody or the lyrics and cannot find a cover version or a hummed tune: a different performance has different peaks. The time alignment, not the number of matching hashes alone, is what makes a match reliable.
why: Avery Wang's Shazam paper (2003) is a standard course reading and 'how does Shazam work' a classic question: https://www.princeton.edu/~cuff/ele201/files/Wang03-shazam.pdf
overlapWith: compression: dropping high-frequency detail from image blocks; this page keeps only spectrogram peaks and matches them, discarding the sound altogether. voice-assistant-wake-word (pool) classifies speech with a trained model; this page is deterministic hashing.
needsSource: none (clips synthesized in the browser with Web Audio; no recordings shipped)
judgeNotes: build 5: STFT, peak picking, pair hashing and an offset histogram over a dozen synthesized clips is the real Wang algorithm at small scale and runs in milliseconds, with no data licensing.
fit-level 4: Constellation hashing with a histogram of time offsets is a superb, distinct mechanism; it honestly needs fourier-transform, a level-2 page, so level 2 is right despite the target mix.
verifyNote: No existing page matches audio. compression keeps spectral coefficients for reconstruction, and this page keeps peak pairs for lookup. Level 2 is honest: a spectrogram needs fourier-transform (level 2), and binary (level 1) is also a valid prerequisite. Short-time FFT, peak picking, combinatorial hashing and an offset histogram over a dozen synthesized clips all run in the browser at interactive rates. No data is needed, since the clips are synthesized. The takeaway and pitfall match Wang (2003): the decisive evidence is time-offset alignment, and the method does not find covers or hummed tunes. The batch target asks for few level-2 topics, but that is a selection question, not a flaw.

title: Distributed hash tables & consistent hashing
interaction: Hash keys and servers onto a ring and watch a lookup walk around it; add or remove a server and count how many keys move, with consistent hashing against the naive modulo rule. Then give each node a finger table and watch lookups finish in a number of hops that grows only logarithmically as the network grows to thousands of nodes; churn nodes in and out and see the ring heal or lose keys depending on how many replicas each key has.
takeaway: Thousands of machines can find any key among them in a dozen hops with no directory, and adding one machine moves only its own share of the keys.
pitfall: Consistent hashing is not fair by default: with one point per server the loads vary widely, which is what virtual nodes fix. A DHT finds where a key lives; it does not make the data durable, replication does.
why: MIT 6.824 Distributed Systems, lecture 20 'DHTs / Chord' https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/archive/6.824-2011/notes/l20.txt
overlapWith: consensus-blockchains: that page makes nodes agree on one log; this one spreads keys across nodes with no agreement at all, which is how a CDN or BitTorrent finds things.
needsSource: none
judgeNotes: build 5: Consistent hashing, Chord finger tables and churn with replicas over thousands of simulated nodes are cheap to simulate, and the logarithmic hop count is a measured result.
fit-level 4: Consistent hashing and Chord finger tables show logarithmic hop counts and minimal key movement, a real distributed-systems mechanism distinct from consensus-blockchains.
verifyNote: Not on the site: consensus-blockchains is about agreeing on a log, internet about packet routing; nothing shows key placement on a ring, the share of keys that move under consistent hashing compared with modulo, or finger-table routing. Its prerequisite hash-tables-bloom-filters is a level-3 candidate in this pool (computing.json), so the levels are consistent. Level 3 is honest: MIT 6.824 and Brown CS168 teach Chord.
